claims.scope: Phase responsibilities and iterative feedback in EPA (1993), UNEP (1996), CML (2001), and EPA (2006); does not constitute a complete lineage or current universal prescription.

claims.text: UNEP's 1996 primer, Life Cycle Assessment: What It Is and How to Do It, employs three overlapping levels of organization within the same volume. Its opening overview introduces the work in three stages, its framework diagram displays four components ending with improvement assessment, and the accompanying legend lists eight operational steps, while the text instructs practitioners to refine the study iteratively. Three stages, four components, and eight steps serve distinct functions—introducing tasks, mapping the conceptual framework, and sequencing operations—and therefore coexist without contradiction in a single publication.
claims.scope: Expository layers in UNEP (1996), printed pp. 3 and 12–13.
caveats: This reflects an interpretation of the publication's expository layers and does not establish equivalence with all subsequent standards.

claims.text: The EPA's May 2006 manual, Life Cycle Assessment: Principles and Practice (EPA/600/R-06/060), consolidates and updates earlier agency guidance. Its abstract still labels the fourth phase "improvement analysis," whereas the main text introduces the four phases using "interpretation" and devotes a full chapter to that phase. Citing phase names from this manual therefore requires specifying whether the reference comes from the abstract or the body text—and the mismatch itself invites examining what analytical work each section actually assigns.
claims.scope: Abstract, body text, and stated source lineage of EPA/600/R-06/060 (May 2006).
caveats: Does not attribute the internal discrepancy to a specific author or editor, nor does it imply that the overall methodology is invalid.

claims.text: The aluminum-foil example in the 1992 CML report shows how calculated outputs guide improvement work. After quantifying solid waste, the authors first trace which activities generate that waste and then examine how total waste responds when process parameters change. Turning favorable numerical results into an implementable option still requires verifying technical feasibility and re-comparing the redesigned system against the baseline. The sections that follow trace the evidence supporting each of those judgments.
claims.scope: Conditions linking calculation, design proposals, and implementation in the 1992 CML hypothetical aluminum-foil example.

claims.text: That example comes from Environmental Life Cycle Assessment of Products, prepared by CML and collaborating teams. Its two volumes—Part I: Guide for operational procedures and Part II: Backgrounds for methodological foundations—belong to the same project; they cross-reference one another and do not represent two independent validations. Although the English title page bears the date October 1992, the preface to the English edition reviews discussions from April 1993. This chapter refers to the work as the 1992 report, while noting that the title-page date alone cannot establish when every English passage was drafted.
claims.scope: Bibliographic identity and preface dating of the two-volume 1992 CML English edition.
caveats: The exact publication date of the English translation is unverified; the English edition does not replace the Dutch original.

claims.text: The 1992 Guide organizes LCA into five components: goal definition, inventory analysis, classification, evaluation, and improvement analysis. Notably, "classification" already encompasses within-category conversion (characterization), aggregation, and normalization, while "evaluation" covers both trade-offs across environmental consequences and checks on the evidentiary basis of conclusions. Comparing this structure with later frameworks therefore requires inspecting the concrete operations behind each heading rather than matching labels alone.
claims.scope: Five components of the 1992 CML Guide and the internal responsibilities of classification and evaluation.

claims.text: In 2001, CML and its collaborators issued Life Cycle Assessment: An Operational Guide to the ISO Standards, separating operational guidance, models and data, and scientific background into distinct parts and requiring explicit disclosure of what aligns with International Organization for Standardization (ISO) standards versus what extends beyond them. Practitioners can follow the operational instructions, verify whether the required models and data are available, and consult the scientific background volume for methodological rationales. When citing specific procedures from the guide, readers must preserve its identity as an operational manual rather than treating every instruction as a binding ISO clause.
claims.scope: Editorial principles and reading guidance in CML (2001) Part 1.
caveats: The guide's explanation of its relationship to ISO does not turn all provisions of the guide into ISO requirements.

claims.text: The relationship between two early workshop records remains unresolved. The 2001 CML guide notes SETAC's involvement in LCA since 1989 and mentions an initial workshop at Smugglers Notch without citing its title, whereas the contemporaneous EPA project page records a technical framework workshop in August 1990 without naming a venue. Each record supports only the facts it explicitly states; available evidence does not establish that both passages refer to the same meeting.
claims.scope: Comparison of event identity between the 2001 CML retrospective account and the 1991 EPA draft project page; insufficient evidence to confirm identity.
caveats: Neither record proves both describe the same event, and no date contradiction for a single event is claimed here.

claims.text: Before any calculation begins, the intended application already shapes the set of candidate alternatives. Part II: Backgrounds uses fresh-milk packaging to illustrate how packaging losses interact with the delivered service, and uses personal mobility to show how commuting patterns, road conditions, and vehicle use constrain viable options. Defining a shared functional reference can exclude other ways of meeting the same need, so analysts and commissioners must state the rationale behind their problem framing.
claims.scope: Intended application, functional framing, and alternative scope in the fresh-milk and mobility examples of CML (1992) Backgrounds.

claims.text: Once the problem is defined, analysts can tailor subsequent steps to what the available evidence already establishes. The 1992 Guide permits omitting classification and environmental-profile trade-offs when the inventory table itself yields an unambiguous comparison. An environmental profile is the set of scores across impact categories; if all category scores and qualitative considerations point in the same direction, normalization and weighting may also be skipped. Even in those streamlined cases, however, analysts must still verify the reliability and validity of data, methods, and conclusions.
claims.scope: Permitted simplifications for unambiguous comparisons and retained conclusion checks in the 1992 CML Guide.

claims.text: Part II: Backgrounds illustrates improvement-target selection by asking whether to prioritize reducing mercury or sulfur dioxide emissions. Deciding which emission to curb first already embeds a bounded judgment about which environmental stressor warrants priority. Improvement work can therefore begin before constructing a full environmental index, provided the improvement plan states explicitly what is prioritized and why.
claims.scope: Selecting improvement targets directly from inventory results in CML (1992) Backgrounds.

claims.text: Comparing assessment frameworks requires tracking three things together: the analytical tasks assigned to each phase, the outputs produced, and how different editions arrange those tasks. A single label can refer to different operations across guides, while the same operation can migrate under a new heading. Tracing such shifts requires verifying dates, editions, and textual relationships separately, and reporting what each source proves on its own whenever links remain unconfirmed.
claims.scope: Analytical method for tracking responsibilities, source lineage, and terminological shifts across historical framework documents.
caveats: This historical-document method is neither an institutional standard nor a complete historical synthesis.

claims.text: UNEP's 1996 guide requires scaling every process's inputs and outputs to the defined functional reference so that upstream electricity generation and downstream manufacturing can be aggregated into one inventory for the same service. It also instructs analysts to retain relevant issues that resist quantification. An inventory output therefore consists not only of numerical tables, but also of an explicit record of known omissions carried forward into later phases.
claims.scope: Inventory scaling and documentation of unquantified items in UNEP (1996); does not constitute a complete lineage or current universal prescription.

claims.text: Replicating the hypothetical worked example in Table 2.3 of the 1992 Guide starts from four unit-process records: electricity generation, aluminum production, aluminum-foil manufacturing, and foil use, scaled to a final demand of 10 sandwich bags. Each unit of electricity activity outputs 1 MJ of electricity while consuming 0.01 kg of aluminum; each unit of aluminum activity outputs 1 kg of aluminum while consuming 50 MJ of electricity; each unit of aluminum-foil activity outputs 1 kg of foil while consuming 1 kg of aluminum and 1 MJ of electricity; and each unit of use activity consumes 1 kg of foil to deliver 100 sandwich bags. Here, one column of the original table represents one unit activity, and its activity level is the scaling factor applied uniformly to that column. These figures were invented by the authors to demonstrate the calculation method rather than measured from real sandwich-bag supply chains.
claims.scope: Hypothetical unit-process model from Table 2.3 of the 1992 CML Guide for a fixed demand of 10 sandwich bags.
caveats: Other environmental rows in the original table are not compared here; only the selected solid-waste balance is reconstructed.

claims.text: Working backward from final demand, 10 sandwich bags require 0.1 units of the use activity and therefore 0.1 units of the aluminum-foil activity. Upstream supply, however, cannot be solved in a single pass because electricity generation consumes aluminum while aluminum production consumes electricity. Denoting the electricity activity level by x and the aluminum activity level by y, the process records yield the coupled balance equations x = 50y + 0.1 and y = 0.01x + 0.1. The 0.1 terms reflect the foil activity's direct demand for 0.1 MJ of electricity and 0.1 kg of aluminum, which equal 0.1 activity units because each unit of electricity outputs 1 MJ and each unit of aluminum outputs 1 kg. Solving the system simultaneously gives x = 10.2 and y = 0.202, balancing total supply and demand across all intermediate flows.
claims.scope: Economic-flow balance of the hypothetical aluminum-foil model; excludes real-world operating conditions.

claims.text: With all four activity levels known, solid waste can be tallied activity by activity. The original table assigns 2 kg, 10 kg, 0 kg, and 1 kg of solid waste per unit of electricity, aluminum, aluminum-foil, and use activity, respectively. Multiplying by the corresponding activity levels gives 20.4 kg, 2.02 kg, 0 kg, and 0.1 kg, for a total of 22.52 kg of solid waste. This sum aggregates a single inventory flow; it does not yet evaluate waste composition, treatment pathways, or resulting environmental damage.
claims.scope: Total solid-waste mass in the hypothetical aluminum-foil model without impact assessment.

claims.text: The printed equations allow independent recalculation of the activity levels, yet line-by-line checking uncovers an internal discrepancy: one intermediate determinant printed in the 1992 Guide disagrees with the equations and activity levels shown on the same page. The accompanying calculation appendix preserves both the printed value and the value obtained directly from the equations. Available source pages pinpoint the discrepancy but do not establish how it arose.
claims.scope: Equation-level audit of the hypothetical aluminum-foil example and discrepancy in a printed intermediate determinant.
caveats: Synthesizes only the cited example and recalculation premises; does not prove full methodological replication or real-world environmental improvement.

claims.text: The 22.52 kg solid-waste total conceals where the waste originates until the four contributions are disaggregated. Recomputing from the model data shows that electricity generation accounts for approximately 90.586% of total solid waste (20.4 kg of 22.52 kg); at the same time, 10.1 MJ of the 10.2 MJ of generated electricity—approximately 99.020%—feeds aluminum production. Most solid waste in this model is thus booked directly to electricity generation, whose output primarily serves aluminum smelting. The 1992 Guide terms this tracking "dominance analysis," because it recovers process-level contributions hidden in aggregated inventory totals.
claims.scope: Direct process contributions and upstream input tracing in the hypothetical aluminum-foil model.

claims.text: Once waste sources are located, analysts can test how the system reacts to small shifts in process data. Because electricity requires aluminum and aluminum requires electricity, altering a single coefficient can propagate across multiple activities. The 1992 Guide calls this local evaluation around the baseline state "marginal analysis." Part II: Backgrounds expresses each response as the ratio of the relative change in output to the relative change in a parameter, enabling comparison across parameters with different physical units. Parameters with large responses flag both potential levers for improvement and priority targets for data verification.
claims.scope: Use of local relative response analysis for design guidance and data checking in both 1992 CML volumes.

claims.text: In the aluminum-foil model, direct solid waste comes predominantly from electricity generation, yet on a percentage basis the largest local response in absolute magnitude belongs to the aluminum output coefficient. Contribution (dominance) analysis decomposes the existing total across activities, whereas local response (marginal) analysis measures sensitivity around the baseline state. Any finite parameter change requires re-solving the balance equations—and even when the re-solved result closely tracks the local linear approximation, analysts must still verify whether the change is feasible in real production.
claims.scope: Distinction among dominance, local response, and finite parameter changes in the fixed hypothetical aluminum-foil model.
caveats: Synthesizes only the cited example and recalculation premises; does not prove full methodological replication or real-world environmental improvement.

claims.text: After totaling waste or emissions, analysts must examine which environmental problems those flows affect. UNEP's 1996 guide first links environmental stressors to relevant problem categories, applies characterization models to express contributions as category indicators, and uses normalization to supply a reference scale. Deciding how much weight each environmental problem deserves, however, involves preferences and social values: even when multiple categories are expressed on a common display scale, normalized numbers alone cannot settle trade-offs.
claims.scope: Characterization, normalization, and value judgments in UNEP (1996); does not constitute a complete lineage or current universal prescription.

claims.text: The 1992 Guide uses two hypothetical office chairs to illustrate cross-category trade-offs. One chair achieves a lower acidification score, while the other achieves a lower human toxicity score. Alongside the table, the authors note that wood data are incomplete, volatile organic compound (VOC) estimates are unreliable, and other aspects lack data entirely. The two categories thus favor opposite choices while data gaps constrain the evidentiary basis for any trade-off.
claims.scope: Environmental-profile comparison and data limitations for two hypothetical office chairs in the 1992 CML Guide.

claims.text: To normalize the chair results, the 1992 Guide divides each chair's effect score by a reference region's annual contribution rate computed with the same classification model, producing a ratio expressed in years. The chair example relies on hypothetical global reference data, and the Guide acknowledges that complete reference totals are often unavailable, permitting analysts to omit normalization when necessary. Although normalization places different categories on a shared temporal scale, summing them across distinct environmental problems still requires an explicit justification for the trade-off.
claims.scope: Dimensions and data conditions of annual-contribution normalization in the 1992 CML Guide.
caveats: Uses only the procedural and qualitative relationships in the original example; does not supply missing annual reference totals or claim item-by-item numerical closure across the two chair tables.

claims.text: In the chair example, representatives of the commissioner and the research team form an evaluation panel to compare Alternative 1 and Alternative 2. The panel observes that Alternative 1 performs better on more indicators while Alternative 2 leads on the more important toxicity indicator; because both alternatives contribute substantially to acidification, however, the panel ultimately selects Alternative 1 for its lower acidification score. The example illustrates how available data and stated priorities shape a specific decision, without establishing default weights or a universal ranking for real office chairs.
claims.scope: Qualitative panel trade-off in the 1992 CML Guide chair example; not a real-world product recommendation.

claims.text: Trade-offs can also be stated through explicit quantitative weights. The 1992 Guide discusses multiplying category effect scores by assigned weights and summing them so that external readers can inspect and recalculate the choice, yet it supplies no ready-to-use weight set. Part II: Backgrounds remarks that such quantitative methods were "not included in the Guide," a statement that does not fully square with the presence of that section in the Guide. Both passages are retained as written; the texts alone do not establish what "not included" was intended to mean.
claims.scope: Divergent descriptions of quantitative multi-criteria analysis (MCA) methods and weighting inputs across the two 1992 CML volumes.

claims.text: Evaluation in the 1992 Guide also tests the evidentiary foundation of conclusions. Reliability checks examine how data uncertainty affects calculated outcomes, whereas validity checks revisit methodological choices such as functional definition, system boundaries, and allocation. Here, "validity" pertains to assumptions and modeling consistency; independently confirming real-world environmental outcomes requires separate empirical evidence. Depending on what these checks uncover, analysts may need to gather additional data or narrow the applicability of their conclusions.
claims.scope: Named meanings of reliability and validity checks in the 1992 CML Guide.

claims.text: Part II: Backgrounds uses a crockery comparison to demonstrate why evaluation must revisit problem definition. Defining the service by number of drinks versus beverage volume, or deciding whether metal spoons and plastic stirrers fall inside the system boundary, can alter the comparison. The text also compares cumulative scores in a single effect category over equal numbers of uses: disposable crockery accumulates its per-use score linearly with each use, whereas reusable crockery combines a fixed manufacturing burden with cumulative per-use burdens. Where those two curves intersect within feasible reuse counts, that crossover point depends on the relative sizes of those contributions. Because the source pages present only the check logic and symbolic relations—without empirical parameters or actual category crossover points—they cannot declare either crockery option superior in practice.
claims.scope: Summary of the crockery comparison and within-category crossover logic in CML (1992) Backgrounds.

claims.text: Choosing between the two office chairs requires justifying why an increase in one environmental burden is accepted to reduce another; auditing the crockery comparison tests whether a comparison still holds when data or methodological choices shift. Explicitly stated preferences can still be fragile under altered assumptions, while a technically robust comparison still requires value judgments to resolve trade-offs. Because the 1992 Guide houses both tasks under "evaluation," readers must examine which type of evaluation a study actually performed.
claims.scope: Comparison between value trade-offs and result checks inside the 1992 CML evaluation component.

claims.text: For product designers, an environmental profile serves as a map for locating improvement options. UNEP's 1996 guide derives design guidelines and candidate modifications from impact hotspots, screens them against cost and performance requirements, and checks for unintended side effects—an order aligned with its stated goals of cleaner production and cleaner consumption. Such work can surface vetted improvement directions, but candidate redesigns must still be compared against the baseline for their intended use.
claims.scope: Design-oriented improvement sequence in UNEP (1996); does not constitute a complete lineage or current universal prescription.

claims.text: Raising an output coefficient in a mathematical model is not the same as improving yield in a factory. Part II: Backgrounds notes that holding steel input fixed while increasing rolled-steel output can point toward technically impossible changes. Holding other coefficients constant helps identify sensitive levers, yet any real engineering modification requires checking which inputs and emissions co-vary with the process and whether the proposed change is physically feasible.
claims.scope: Distinction between local sensitivity analysis and engineering feasibility in CML (1992) Backgrounds.

claims.text: A soot-reduction example in Part II: Backgrounds underscores why isolated parameter tweaks are misleading. Lowering soot emissions by altering combustion temperature simultaneously changes resource use, other air emissions, and solid residues, whereas installing flue-gas scrubbing introduces an entirely new unit process. Simply reducing the soot entry in an inventory table captures the full consequence of neither measure. Backgrounds therefore requires encoding the concrete engineering measure into a redesigned system and re-comparing it with the original—recognizing that the redesign may perform either better or worse overall.
claims.scope: Coupled parameter shifts, added processes, and re-comparison in the soot example of CML (1992) Backgrounds.

claims.text: UNEP's 1996 coffee-packaging example shows how cutting packaging mass can shift burdens elsewhere. If thinner packaging increases breakage during distribution, the lost coffee can offset or even outweigh the material savings. A study must track both effects simultaneously and verify whether the delivered service changed; the optimal thickness of any real package must still be determined from its actual protective performance.
claims.scope: Trade-off between packaging reduction and product loss in UNEP (1996); does not constitute a complete lineage or current universal prescription.

claims.text: Both the 1992 Guide and Backgrounds accordingly separate generating improvement options, selecting candidates, and implementing changes: analysts first identify potential modifications, screen them against technical, financial, and market constraints, define concrete product variants, compare those variants against the baseline design, and iterate as needed. Environmental assessment supplies comparative evidence, while adoption depends on broader organizational and market conditions. Comparing later frameworks involves checking whether these tasks remain present and which phases house them.
claims.scope: Innovation loop and division of responsibilities in the 1992 CML Guide and Backgrounds.

claims.text: The 2001 CML operational guide states explicitly that it revises the 1992 report in response to ISO and SETAC developments as well as Dutch user needs. It adopts the four-phase architecture—goal and scope definition, inventory analysis, impact assessment, and interpretation—while providing its own operational sequence and emphasizing iteration in practice. This authorial statement establishes the link between the two editions, though attributing specific textual revisions to particular external influences requires separate evidence.
claims.scope: Author-stated revision relationship and external drivers in CML (2001); not a complete causal lineage.

claims.text: Comparing the 1992 and 2001 editions also requires accounting for how each edition divides its volumes. The 1992 report separated Guide and Backgrounds, while the 2001 edition separates operational guidance, models and data, and scientific background. In 2001, the Scientific Background volume discusses procedural organization centrally, whereas the operational Guide embeds procedural steps within each phase for ready lookup. The placement or repetition of a heading alone therefore cannot prove that the underlying analytical work expanded or shrank.
claims.scope: Volume roles across the 1992 and 2001 CML editions and procedural layout within the 2001 edition.

claims.text: In the 2001 Scientific Background volume, analysts first define a preliminary scope and then finalize data categories, cut-off criteria, and data quality during inventory analysis, disclosing those choices in reporting and interpretation. Although the guide prioritizes structural decisions that alter product systems over the long term, it still distinguishes a detailed baseline inventory from market-mechanism extensions discussed separately. Determining whether a given study actually modeled market responses requires inspecting the model it used.
claims.scope: Placement of preliminary scope, detailed baseline inventory, and market-mechanism extensions in CML (2001).

claims.text: The 2001 CML guide also specifies what metadata must travel with each phase's outputs. Inventory results include not only numerical tables, but also unquantified items and data-quality documentation; impact assessment produces an environmental profile. Whenever omissions could alter rankings or data represent only narrow conditions, interpretation must retain that accompanying information to judge under what conditions the conclusions remain robust.
claims.scope: Accompanying metadata required for inventory and impact outputs in CML (2001); does not constitute a complete lineage or current universal prescription.

claims.text: The 2001 Scientific Background volume places consistency and completeness checks ahead of contribution, perturbation, and sensitivity analyses: if data already suffer from severe mismatches or gaps, finer response calculations may fail to answer the original question. The authors note that this sequence modifies the contemporaneous ISO arrangement as they describe it. The operational Guide directs analysts to judge the significance of mismatches and gaps—returning to earlier phases when corrections are possible, or stating explicit applicability limits in the conclusions when they are not.
claims.scope: Authors' rationale for sequencing consistency, completeness, and subsequent analyses in CML (2001).
caveats: The comparison with ISO relies solely on the 2001 CML guide's own account; it does not substitute for the original ISO text or represent independent verification of current ISO clauses.

claims.text: The objects of the analytical checks in CML 2001 Part 2a must also be distinguished carefully. Contribution analysis decomposes existing results across sources; perturbation analysis applies small variations around the baseline to parameters such as process data or characterization factors, expressing response as the ratio of relative output change to relative parameter change; sensitivity analysis deliberately alters data, models, or methodological choices—such as switching allocation methods—to test robustness, with perturbation analysis capable of informing it rather than standing wholly apart; and uncertainty analysis estimates output error from empirical input uncertainty ranges. Although the guide regards perturbation analysis as useful, it permits both simplified and detailed studies to omit it because dedicated software was not yet widely available. Listing a method, recommending it, possessing workable software, and executing it in a study are four distinct facts.
claims.scope: Operational definitions and software-availability conditions for contribution, perturbation, sensitivity, and uncertainty analysis in CML (2001) Part 2a.
caveats: Preserves the conditions stated in the 2001 edition; historical software availability does not describe current practice.

claims.text: Even under the 2001 edition, the weighting dilemma seen in the office-chair example has no universal resolution. The Scientific Background volume reviews multi-criteria analysis (MCA) without recommending a universal weight set. Published weights may match different impact categories and characterization models, and some combine environmental modeling with value judgments in ways that prevent multiplying them onto another category profile. The operational Guide treats weighting as optional and paraphrases the contemporaneous ISO 14042 restriction against weighting in public comparative assertions. When weights are applied, studies must still report unweighted conclusions alongside omitted or uncharacterized items.
claims.scope: Compatibility, optional status, and reporting rules for weighting in CML (2001).
caveats: The historical ISO 14042 relationship is paraphrased from the 2001 CML guide and does not represent independent verification of current ISO clauses.

claims.text: Comparing concrete operations reveals how tasks were reorganized between 1992 and 2001. Both 1992 dominance analysis and 2001 contribution analysis decompose existing totals into contributing sources, and both early marginal analysis and later perturbation analysis examine responses to parameter changes—a task-level comparison that does not imply full mathematical equivalence across editions. Early reliability and validity checks, targeting data uncertainty and methodological choices respectively, continue inside the more detailed 2001 interpretation steps without mapping one-to-one onto the newer subheadings. In 2001, weighting sits inside impact assessment as an optional step, while the dual use of local response analysis for both design guidance and data checking already appeared in 1992. These checks support conclusions and recommendations, whereas engineering screening and real-world implementation remain separate tasks.
claims.scope: Conditional task-level comparison between CML (1992) and CML (2001); does not claim full phase-by-phase equivalence.

claims.text: CML's 2001 operational guide assigns two core outputs to interpretation: evaluating the quality and robustness of inventory and impact results, and formulating conclusions and recommendations, which may include improvement directions. Using a hypothetical packaging example, the guide cautions that a study designed to identify improvement opportunities cannot be repurposed directly to claim superiority over competing packaging; any comparative assertion requires study conditions designed for that comparison.
claims.scope: Dual outputs of interpretation and comparative-claim limits in CML (2001); does not constitute a complete lineage or current universal prescription.

claims.text: EPA's 2006 manual translates these requirements into a structured checking sequence: first identify significant issues, then perform completeness, sensitivity, and consistency checks. Wherever gaps or inconsistencies affect a comparison, analysts must either expand the study or document how those limitations bound the conclusions. These checks interrogate the inferential basis of the study: whether conclusions survive changes in key assumptions, whether differences between options stem from data or boundary asymmetries, and whether available evidence actually supports the judgment requested.
claims.scope: Interpretation checking procedures in EPA (2006); does not constitute a complete lineage or current universal prescription.

claims.text: Even after completing all checks, ranking alternatives may remain unsupported. The 2006 EPA manual notes that recommendations can support either option selection or process improvement; when data limitations, model choices, or uncertainty prevent a defensible ranking, a study can still document each option's favorable and unfavorable health and environmental effects and identify where they occur. A conditional environmental judgment is a valid and useful outcome in its own right without forcing a ranking that the evidence cannot sustain.
claims.scope: Scope of recommendations and non-ranking outcomes in EPA (2006); does not constitute a complete lineage or current universal prescription.

claims.text: Recommendations must remain tied to the specific service analyzed. The 2001 CML Scientific Background volume uses packaging of different volumes to warn that even when materials and product names appear similar, extrapolating conclusions requires demonstrating how volume changes the delivered service, material inputs, and related activities, backed by separate justification. A favorable finding must first specify the exact service and system it covers rather than being transferred automatically to another package.
claims.scope: Limits on conclusions, recommendations, and cross-system extrapolation in CML (2001).

claims.text: Issuing a recommendation in a report does not mean stakeholders have reached a decision. The 2001 CML Scientific Background volume separates analytical information, the decision made from it, and the outcome after implementation. Environmental profiles, trade-offs, and error analyses furnish reasons for action alongside economic, policy, and implementation considerations. Whether an option is adopted—and whether adoption delivers actual environmental gains—each require separate records and evidence.
claims.scope: Distinction among analytical results, decision conclusions, and post-implementation outcomes in CML (2001) Scientific Background.

claims.text: Part 2a of the 2001 CML guide recalls a dispute over evaluation criteria under the first Dutch Packaging Covenant. Switching from single-use to refillable packaging was conditioned on demonstrating substantially lower environmental damage, yet participants had not agreed sufficiently upfront on which environmental aspects to include or which decision rules to apply. A supervisory committee later established criteria and requested additional studies for several comparisons. Consumer organizations maintained that the advantage of refillable polycarbonate over milk cartons had been demonstrated, whereas industry representatives argued that reductions in waste and potential eutrophication were insufficient. Because this account is the guide authors' retrospective summary, it cannot serve as direct primary evidence of the original covenant, committee minutes, or subsequent implementation.
claims.scope: Retrospective case of the first Dutch Packaging Covenant in CML (2001) Part 2a; implementation not independently verified.

claims.text: The Dutch packaging dispute exposes two distinct requirements: whether the data suffice to support a comparison, and by what criteria stakeholders agree to decide. Adding another impact indicator can supply more information, yet it cannot negotiate decision rules on the participants' behalf; conversely, even agreed criteria cannot spare the underlying data and inferences from scrutiny. Clarifying both evidentiary and procedural bases is necessary before an environmental profile can support a transparent joint decision.
claims.scope: Relationship between analytical checks and stakeholder decision criteria in the Dutch Packaging Covenant case.

claims.text: Framework evolution is therefore best described through concrete analytical tasks rather than simple phase replacement. Early inventory guidance already incorporated iterative feedback, and later interpretation phases still generate improvement recommendations. Diagnosis and design identify what can be changed; checking and interpretation determine what conclusions the current evidence can support. Different guides sequence or group these tasks differently, and this body of texts alone does not establish that the entire LCA community followed a single uniform trajectory.
claims.scope: Task-based comparison of framework evolution across EPA (1993), UNEP (1996), CML (2001), and EPA (2006); does not constitute a complete lineage or current universal prescription.

claims.text: Readers can apply the same task-based lens to evaluate what any study can legitimately claim. In the worked coating case (Wall Service Comparison), two coating systems delivering the same wall service are compared under explicit assumptions: gas quantities are calculated first, and climate indicators are derived next through a characterization model. Comparing the two coatings further requires fixing shared parameters and stating decision criteria, while recommending commercial products requires empirical performance and environmental data. Each judgment rests on its own relations and evidence rather than following automatically from earlier calculations.
claims.scope: Applying task-based framework criteria to read study claims, illustrated via Wall Service Comparison.

claims.text: Extending this historical arc to four contemporary operational guides—CML 2001/2002 (Part 2a), the International Reference Life Cycle Data System (ILCD) Handbook (2010), the European Union (EU) Product Environmental Footprint (PEF) method (Commission Recommendation (EU) 2021/2279, Annex I), and the Greenhouse Gas (GHG) Protocol Product Life Cycle Accounting and Reporting Standard (2011)—reveals a shared structural backbone. Each begins by defining purpose, analytical reference, and system boundaries, then compiles an inventory, calculates impacts, and refines assumptions iteratively through completeness, sensitivity, and consistency checks. CML 2001 (Part 2a) follows the four ISO phases—goal and scope, inventory, impact assessment, and interpretation—prefaced by a first chapter on project procedure management (five chapters in total). ILCD 2010 (§4, Figure 4) maps those four phases as iterative refinement loops that screen hotspots with generic data before focusing effort on dominant processes. Although the GHG Protocol Product Standard (§3.1, Figure 3.1) sequences its chapters around business goals, principles, scope, boundaries, data quality, allocation, uncertainty, assurance, reporting, and reduction targets, it still operates on the same closed loop of problem framing, accounting, and verification.
claims.scope: Cross-framework comparison of phase organization and iterative structure across CML (2001) Part 2a (pp. 3–4), ILCD (2010) (§4, Figure 4), and GHG Protocol Product Standard (2011) (§3.1, Figure 3.1).

claims.text: The first major divergence among the four frameworks lies in what decision context a study addresses and when public cross-product comparative assertions are permitted. ILCD 2010 (§1) routes studies upfront by decision context: micro-level decision support (Situation A) assumes no structural changes in background production capacity; meso/macro-level strategic decision support (Situation B) accounts for structural capacity changes; and purely descriptive accounting (Situation C) does not model economic consequences, splitting further into C1 (including credit for external recycling or interactions) and C2 (excluding such credit)—choices that directly alter system boundaries and life cycle inventory (LCI) modeling rules. EU PEF 2021 (Annex I Definitions and §1) tightens comparability to the product-category level, distinguishing general comparisons from comparative assertions and permitting either only when conducted under a valid Product Environmental Footprint Category Rule (PEFCR). By contrast, the GHG Protocol Product Standard (§§1.5, 5.3.2, and Appendix A) is designed for longitudinal emissions tracking of a single product, explicitly does not support ISO 14044 comparative assertions of overall environmental superiority, and requires separate harmonized product rules for any cross-product comparison.
claims.scope: Cross-framework comparison of decision-context routing and comparative-assertion gates in ILCD (2010) (§1), EU PEF (2021) (Annex I Definitions and §1), and GHG Protocol Product Standard (2011) (§1.5, §5.3.2, Appendix A).

claims.text: A second substantive divergence concerns impact-category coverage and whether results may be weighted into a single score. CML 2001 (Part 2a, pp. 48, 75, 77–78) establishes midpoint problem-oriented multi-category characterization as its baseline, strongly recommends normalization to inspect relative magnitudes, and leaves grouping and weighting as optional extensions with no baseline method; it also paraphrases the ISO 14042 prohibition against weighting in publicly disclosed comparative assertions, forcing analysts to drop public comparison, keep the study internal, or omit weighting. EU PEF 2021 (Annex I §3.2 Table 2 and §§5.1–5.2) adopts strong harmonization: it mandates all 16 Environmental Footprint (EF) impact categories with no exclusions, followed by mandatory normalization and weighting and optional aggregation into a single score (reported both with and without the use stage). The GHG Protocol Product Standard accounts solely for greenhouse gases as a single impact category—avoiding cross-category trade-off disputes, yet offering no coverage of toxicity, acidification, water use, or land use and therefore providing no basis to claim that a product is environmentally superior overall.
claims.scope: Cross-framework comparison of impact-category coverage, normalization, and weighting rules in CML (2001) Part 2a (pp. 48, 75, 77–78), EU PEF (2021) (Annex I Table 2, §§5.1–5.2), and GHG Protocol Product Standard (2011) (§1.5, §3.1).

claims.text: Interpretation checks and external review governance likewise stratify according to each framework's institutional purpose. CML 2001 (Part 2a, Chapter 5) anchors interpretation in consistency, completeness, and sensitivity or uncertainty evaluation, requiring analysts to report result bandwidths and limitations before offering recommendations. ILCD 2010 (Chapter 11) requires defining the review type during scoping to verify methodological compliance, scientific validity, data appropriateness, and candid disclosure of limitations, establishing ISO 14040/14044 as the minimum floor pending dedicated review rules. EU PEF 2021 (Annex I §8.1) imposes a strict external gate: any external communication of study results or partial findings triggers mandatory independent verification and validation checking model, data, and report consistency. The GHG Protocol Product Standard (Chapter 12, §§12.1–12.2) adopts the assurance model familiar from financial and carbon accounting—defining a three-party structure of reporting company, stakeholders, and assurer—and requires first-party or third-party assurance of the product carbon inventory, which is not equivalent to multi-indicator LCA peer-panel review.
claims.scope: Cross-framework comparison of interpretation checks, critical review, and assurance governance in CML (2001) Part 2a (Chapter 5), ILCD (2010) (Chapter 11), EU PEF (2021) (Annex I §8.1), and GHG Protocol Product Standard (2011) (§§12.1–12.2).

claims.text: These differences are not merely stylistic variations in table-of-contents layout; they directly reshape a study's outputs, compliance thresholds, and decision risks. Consider a manufacturer preparing a competitor comparison for the EU market. Completing a single-category GHG Protocol inventory with first-party assurance omits 15 non-climate impact categories and lacks institutional eligibility for comparative assertions. Switching to the CML 2001 detailed baseline delivers a multi-category midpoint profile, yet without harmonized category rules and public weighting authorization, competing studies can still diverge on boundaries, allocation, and background databases. Adopting EU PEF 2021 under a valid PEFCR with independent verification yields a comparable 16-category profile and a single weighted score, at the cost of accepting fixed categories, preset normalization and weighting factors, and higher disclosure and verification expenses. Under ILCD 2010, evaluating a policy that alters grid or raw-material capacity under Situation A (micro-level) rather than Situation B (meso/macro-level) misdirects inventory modeling from the very start.
claims.scope: Practical effects of framework selection on study outputs, comparability eligibility, and decision risk across the four open-access guides.

claims.text: The evidentiary boundaries of this cross-framework comparison must be stated explicitly. Every comparison above was verified directly against four open-access primary texts: CML 2001 Part 2a, ILCD 2010 Detailed Guidance, Annex I of EU Commission Recommendation (EU) 2021/2279, and the GHG Protocol Product Standard (2011). Copyrighted paywalled full texts of ISO 14040/14044:2006 (governed by the uniform verification boundary stated in the Reading Guide) and unacquired 1991 and 1993 SETAC workshop proceedings are not reconstructed without direct verification. Equally important, completing any framework's phases and passing external review or assurance confirms adherence to that framework's procedural and disclosure rules alone; it neither supplies missing measured emissions data nor replaces the functional-reference, inventory-boundary, allocation, impact-modeling, and uncertainty checks developed in subsequent parts of this monograph.
claims.scope: Paywalled-standard boundaries, unacquired-historical-source boundaries, and epistemic limits of procedural compliance for this cross-framework comparison.
caveats: Full paywalled clauses of ISO 14040/14044 and the original 1991/1993 SETAC workshop proceedings were not directly verified in this section.

claims.text: Understanding how external studies actually use methodological guidance requires auditing concrete citations and calculations. In January 1994, a Battelle team working under contract for the EPA published a lithographic-printing pollution-prevention screening report (EPA/600/R-94/157) that cites the 1992 CML Guide among its sources of characterization values while defining its own scoring bins and aggregation rules. Auditing the resulting scores reveals far more than scanning a bibliography: it shows whether cited values match the screening operations and what transformations occurred along the way.
claims.scope: Named use of 1992 CML Guide data in the 1994 EPA/Battelle lithographic-printing screening report.

claims.text: First, the numerical quantities in the two reports represent different constructs. In the 1992 CML Guide, photochemical ozone creation potential (POCP) takes an equal mass of ethylene emitted to air as its reference, converting airborne substance emissions into ethylene equivalents; the ranges printed alongside the table reflect European scenarios and differing time horizons, citing 1991 United Nations Economic Commission for Europe (UNECE) material. The 1994 EPA screening report maps those values into its own numerical intervals to assign ordinal bin scores. Although relative contribution factors connect to scores through value selection and binning, the resulting bin scores do not preserve the full physical meaning of the underlying factors.
claims.scope: Distinction between the ethylene-mass reference in the 1992 CML Guide and the ordinal screening scores in EPA (1994).
caveats: Verifies definitions and attribution in the 1992 CML Guide without treating the cited UNECE original as directly read; printed ranges carry no probabilistic status.

claims.text: Checking acetone and toluene tests how actual solvent scores align with the cited source. The 1994 EPA report states that solvent POCP scores are taken directly from the examples listed in its binning table. In the 1992 CML Guide, the point values are 0.178 for acetone and 0.563 for toluene. Mapped into EPA's intervals, 0.178 falls in the 0.051–0.500 bin (score 5) and 0.563 falls in the 0.501–0.999 bin (score 3); EPA's operational solvent table likewise reports 5 and 3. This match shows that both CML point values are compatible with EPA's bins, yet it neither establishes the exact numerical precision the authors consulted nor proves that every entry was drawn exclusively from a single source.
claims.scope: Alignment between 1992 CML Guide point values and 1994 EPA base bins and reported solvent scores for acetone and toluene.

claims.text: Converting continuous factors into bin scores can also obscure underlying ranges. The scenario values printed for toluene in the 1992 CML Guide span two different EPA bins, and the Guide explains that range in terms of scenarios and time horizons rather than defining it as a sampling probability or confidence interval. In addition, EPA's printed adjacent intervals leave numerical gaps without specifying how values falling inside those gaps should be assigned. For any value lying in an unspecified gap, its bin assignment must remain explicitly undetermined.
claims.scope: Bounded comparison of CML toluene scenario ranges against printed EPA base scoring bins.
caveats: Synthesizes only the cited example and recalculation premises; does not prove full methodological replication or real-world environmental improvement.

claims.text: Methane, by contrast, does not match the 1992 CML Guide point value. The Guide lists 0.007 for methane, which falls inside EPA's 0.006–0.050 bin (score 7), yet EPA lists methane as an illustrative example in the ≤ 0.005 bin (score 9). Methane appears only as a table-legend example, whereas acetone and toluene appear in the operational solvent table—two distinct categories of evidence. Because the inspected passages do not explain this discrepancy, agreement for two solvents cannot be generalized into proof of a uniform single source across all examples.
claims.scope: Unexplained mismatch between the 1992 CML point value for methane and its placement in the 1994 EPA binning example.

claims.text: The 1994 EPA screening procedure also adjusts scores for emission quantities and local ozone attainment status, and discusses equal-weighted aggregation across criteria alongside data-quality limitations. This chapter recalculates only the base bins. Interpreting those scores requires retaining the physical reference, binning rules, site-specific adjustments, and aggregation weights; determining how much actual ground-level ozone or environmental damage changed still requires modeling those consequences directly.
claims.scope: Boundaries of base binning, site adjustments, and equal-weighted aggregation in the 1994 EPA screening report.
caveats: No rule is provided for assigning unrounded values that fall in the gaps between printed bin boundaries; no interpolation or gap-filling is performed.

claims.text: The 1994 EPA screening report and the 1993 EPA inventory guide also share an institutional lineage: both involve authors including Tolle and Vigon, operate under the same Battelle contract (68-CO-0003) and EPA project officer, and the 1994 report cites the 1993 guide for methodological background. Although the two documents serve different purposes, recurring statements across them do not necessarily constitute independent corroboration. The concrete evidence the screening report contributes here is how external characterization values are transformed into scores and which information is lost in that conversion.
claims.scope: Authorship, contract lineage, and specific data adoption linking EPA (1993) and EPA (1994).

claims.text: Terminological crosswalks across institutions likewise require direct verification. The preface to the English edition of the 1992 CML Guide maps its own "classification" to classification and characterization in a cited 1993 SETAC draft, and maps "evaluation" to "valuation," without detailing how reliability checks, engineering feasibility, or implementation correspond item by item. That preface reflects the CML authors' reading of the draft before them; verifying whether two sets of procedures actually coincide requires inspecting the SETAC original and comparing both workflows directly.
claims.scope: CML English-edition preface crosswalk against a cited 1993 SETAC draft.

claims.text: Taken together, these historical and contemporary sources show how assessment frameworks link inventory accounting, impact indicators, design options, and recommendations so that each judgment rests on commensurate evidence. Between 1992 and 2001, CML preserved the links among diagnosis, verification checks, and improvement while reorganizing specific steps; the 1994 external screening study demonstrates that downstream users may extract selected factors and embed them in their own scoring rules. Next, we examine life cycle assessment's role in cleaner production: why it was enlisted for pollution prevention and what it can actually deliver in practice.
claims.scope: Synthesis of framework responsibilities supported by the primary texts, named examples, and evidentiary boundaries examined in this chapter.

claims.text: Before comparing two paints for a wall, an analyst must state what condition the wall is expected to reach and how long that condition must last. Mass in kilograms records how much paint is purchased, but coverage and protective performance must be specified separately. The 2010 International Reference Life Cycle Data System (ILCD) Handbook defines a functional unit through four elements: what is delivered, how much, how well, and for how long. This chapter groups those four elements as the service requirement. Fixing them first makes it possible to determine how much of each paint is needed for a fair comparison.
claims.scope: Entry point for service-based comparisons constructed from the ILCD 2010 functional-unit specification

claims.text: Identical dimensions do not guarantee an identical service. The 2006 U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) guidance illustrates this with thermal insulation: two materials of the same area and thickness can differ substantially in thermal resistance. If the goal is to reduce heat flow, the comparison must first align the required reduction in heat transfer. This example serves as a pedagogical illustration in the guidance; the thermal performance of real products still requires empirical product data.
claims.scope: Historical context from the named guidance excerpt; does not substitute for current standards or product-level verification
caveats: Pedagogical examples do not provide empirical performance or environmental comparison evidence for real products.

claims.text: Reporting environmental burdens "per use" leaves the comparison incomplete unless it is clear whether both options perform the same task. A service requirement should specify who uses the product, what level of performance is required, how long that performance lasts, and which differences the study accepts. Two alternatives may differ in technical attributes so long as the analyst explains how their relevant service is aligned. The ILCD Handbook also discusses comparing partially comparable options, provided that the underlying judgments and preferences are stated explicitly. Whenever an accepted difference can affect the conclusion, the main text must explain why it was accepted.
claims.scope: Conditional interpretation of service alternatives; partially comparable options still require explicit judgments and preferences
caveats: Discussion of partially comparable options does not waive specific comparative-assertion rules, Product Category Rules, or other applicable requirements.

claims.text: How a service is defined determines which activities enter the inventory. The 2006 EPA guidance compares bar soap and liquid soap by first asking how much of each is needed for an equivalent hand-washing event; matching mass or volume alone cannot answer that question. If the liquid soap also provides moisturizing benefits, the guidance asks two follow-up questions: whether moisturizing is relevant to the study goal, and whether consumers actually realize that benefit. When both conditions hold, the bar-soap alternative must account for adding hand lotion so that it is compared against a system delivering both cleansing and moisturizing.
claims.scope: Historical context from the named guidance excerpt; does not substitute for current standards or product-level verification

claims.text: Shifting the service from "hand-washing" to "hand-washing plus moisturizing" can pull previously omitted products, packaging, or use-phase activities into the inventory. The analyst must inspect and include those activities rather than merely changing the denominator of the original calculation. The soap example states clear conditions for expanding the boundary; whether other secondary functions should be included still depends on the specific study purpose and how those functions are delivered.
claims.scope: Inference from the conditional pedagogical example; does not claim that every additional function requires system expansion

claims.text: In the wall-coating setting, the analyst first specifies the performance the coating must deliver and then determines how much of each concrete product is needed to achieve it. That conversion depends on spreading rate, service life, use conditions, and maintenance schedules. Only with those conditions specified can a service requirement be translated into the product or service quantities required by each alternative.
claims.scope: Interpretive framework linking functional specification to reference flows
caveats: Conversion can depend on performance, service life, and use conditions; a single product quantity cannot substitute for those premises.

claims.text: Suppose two paints satisfy the same coating and protection requirements over a single maintenance period for a 10 m² wall, requiring 0.20 kg/m² of Paint A or 0.25 kg/m² of Paint B. Multiplying area by application rate yields 2.0 kg of Paint A and 2.5 kg of Paint B. Equivalent performance is an explicit premise of this calculation, and multiplication shows only how much product is needed under those assumptions. If environmental results are reported per kilogram of paint, one must still verify coverage, durability, and maintenance schedules before scaling to the same service.
claims.scope: Author-constructed pedagogical coating-maintenance example; 0.20 × 10 and 0.25 × 10
caveats: Numerical values are explicit assumptions, not measured data or product performance claims; environmental results still require separate calculation.

claims.text: Once the required quantity of each paint is known, the next question is what basis the other quantities in the process data are expressed against. In Part 2a (§2.3.4) of the 2001 CML (Institute of Environmental Sciences, Leiden University) operational guide, the reference flow of an alternative is expressed as the wall area covered by a given paint, while the required paint volume is recorded in the process data. Here the service requirement states the desired wall condition, area provides the quantitative reference for the alternative, and paint volume enters the process dataset—so the reference flow is expressed in terms of area.
claims.scope: Alternative reference basis and process data in the CML 2001 Part 2a §2.3.4 paint example

claims.text: The 2010 ILCD Handbook (§6.4.1) similarly notes two conventions: a reference flow may be expressed directly in terms of the functional unit or as a quantity of product. Which convention is chosen depends on the nature of the product, the intended use of the data, and how the software models the system. Under either convention, the dataset must make clear how all other inputs and outputs are scaled relative to the reference. Even a label reading "1 kg of product" requires checking whether the dataset describes producing 1 kg of product or uses 1 kg of product to represent the function delivered by an alternative.
claims.scope: Use-dependent expression of reference flows in ILCD 2010 §6.4.1

claims.text: When reading the CML and ILCD guides side by side, a practical sequence is to identify the service requirement first, then check what quantity serves as the alternative's reference, and finally inspect the process records needed to deliver it. Both guides use the term "reference flow," yet whether two reference flows are interchangeable depends on what each measures, what role it plays in the study, and whether both can be converted under identical conditions. This sequence is the monograph's synthesis for comparing usage across the two guides.
claims.scope: Author synthesis comparing usage in CML and ILCD; not a unified formal terminology definition

claims.text: In an ILCD Format 1.1 process dataset, the `quantitativeReference` section specifies the basis to which inputs and outputs are scaled. Its type may be a reference flow, a functional unit, another parameter, or a production period. When a production period is selected, the reference is the operating time span represented by the dataset. Seeing this field therefore never justifies assuming that the dataset is automatically normalized to 1 kg of product.
claims.scope: ILCD Format 1.1 process dataset specification

claims.text: When the type is set to `Reference flow(s)`, the `referenceToReferenceFlow` field points to one or more input or output exchanges within the dataset that serve as its reference. This field records an internal pointer to exchanges in the dataset; the product's functional performance is documented separately in text.
claims.scope: ILCD Format 1.1, eDoc 1-1-4-16 and 1-1-4-17

claims.text: To inspect functional performance in the same format, one checks the `functionalUnitOrOther` field. It can record a quantity, name, property or quality, and unit without pointing to any single flow. Even when a dataset uses a reference flow as its quantitative reference, it may also record a functional unit alongside it, allowing one file to store both exchange pointers and performance descriptions. This describes what ILCD Format 1.1 permits a dataset to store; how the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) or other methodologies formally define a functional unit must be checked in their own governing texts.
claims.scope: Quantitative reference documentation in ILCD Format 1.1
caveats: This explains the meaning of the format documentation, not a unified definition across ISO standards or all LCA methods.

claims.text: If Paint B in the 10 m² example also requires a maintenance recoating during the same period, the initial 2.5 kg reflects only the original schedule. One must specify what the maintenance operation entails and recalculate material inputs before assessing environmental performance; if the required surface performance itself changes, the comparison problem must be reframed altogether. Footnote 39 to the ILCD paint example similarly cautions that recoating may require stripping the old layer or applying a future paint formulation. Which processes maintenance alters must be established before multiplying material quantities.
claims.scope: Condition change in the author's 10 m² pedagogical example, contextualized by the ILCD maintenance note
caveats: Does not provide empirical conclusions about real paint performance, recoating frequency, or environmental superiority.

claims.text: Even when a dataset stores both reference-exchange pointers and performance descriptions, the analyst must verify which activities the model actually uses to deliver the service. One can trace product identity, quantity, and unit through the exchange pointer and then inspect the evidence supporting performance and dosage. Product Category Rules (PCR) define declared units in different ways, and software tools represent multi-product demands differently. Both pieces of information may appear in the data record, but whether the model actually applies them must be verified in the modeled processes and links.
claims.scope: Interpretive boundary among data format, functional description, and model execution; makes no claim about specific software behavior
caveats: What a data format can record does not determine solver behavior; specific implementations require independent evidence.

claims.text: Establishing service comparability is only the first check; the systems delivering that service must also be audited. In discussing assertions of environmental superiority or equivalence, CML 2001 paraphrases ISO requirements on system boundaries, data quality, allocation, and impact assessment. ILCD 2010 further details how to check consistency across scenarios, service lives, maintenance, data, and modeling, noting that uncertainty and the set of included impact categories constrain what can be concluded. Even when two alternatives deliver a comparable service, the results may support a difference only on a single indicator; any overall claim must state the impact categories, models, and conditions used.
claims.scope: Bounded synthesis of CML comparative-assertion requirements and ILCD comparative-study conditions
caveats: Selected guidance excerpts do not substitute for verifying the authoritative ISO text, the modeling provisions cited by ILCD, or full study compliance.

claims.text: This monograph divides a comparative assessment into three distinct judgments: how the service requirements of the alternatives are aligned and which differences are accepted; how the model's boundaries and data represent the processes delivering that service; and how strong a difference claim the final results can support. The remainder of this chapter places the first judgment across four major methodological and database frameworks to clarify where functional units, declared units, activity-level reference products, and comparability gates align—and where they diverge.
claims.scope: Analytical proposal dividing comparative studies into service, model, and result layers; not an added formal standard phase

claims.text: Placed side by side, the ILCD Handbook, the European Union Product Environmental Footprint (PEF) method, the Greenhouse Gas Protocol (GHG Protocol) Product Standard, and the ecoinvent v3 Data Quality Guideline all agree that comparing alternatives requires fixing a verifiable quantitative benchmark and separating the service delivered from the physical product quantity needed to deliver it. Yet that consensus holds chiefly for final-product comparisons where all four elements (what, how much, how well, how long) are explicit and boundaries are symmetric. Once a study enters activity-level data modeling, intermediate products with undetermined end uses, service-life rounding, or public comparative assertions, the four frameworks diverge sharply in both division of labor and admissibility thresholds.
claims.scope: Shared premises and divergence points across ILCD, PEF, GHG Protocol, and ecoinvent v3 on functional reference

claims.text: The first structural divergence lies in the analytical layer at which the reference operates. ILCD, PEF, and the GHG Protocol all define service-oriented functional units and reference flows at the study level. By contrast, the ecoinvent v3 Data Quality Guideline operates at the unit-process activity level: rather than prescribing a study-level functional unit, it defines the reference product (or determining product in consequential modeling) as the output whose change in demand directly scales the activity, and records waste-treatment services as negative physical reference products representing the material received. A database reference product therefore specifies only how an individual process is scaled and linked; it cannot stand in directly for a study-level functional unit across competing alternatives.
claims.scope: Layer separation between study-level functional units and activity-level determining reference products in ecoinvent v3

claims.text: The second divergence concerns intermediate products whose downstream uses are not yet fixed. For semi-finished goods or materials entering diverse end uses, both ILCD (such as 1 kg of steel coil) and PEF allow a declared unit accompanied by technical specifications, and ILCD §6.4 explicitly states that a declared unit is not a functional unit: it may be used to compare alternative production routes for the same material, but not to compare different materials on an equal-mass basis. The GHG Protocol Product Standard avoids the term "declared unit" altogether and introduces an overarching "unit of analysis": final products must use a functional unit as their unit of analysis, whereas intermediate products with undetermined downstream functions use a reference flow directly under a cradle-to-gate boundary while disclosing the excluded use and end-of-life stages.
claims.scope: Terminological and methodological divergence between declared units in ILCD/PEF and reference-flow units of analysis for intermediate products in the GHG Protocol

claims.text: The third divergence governs how service requirements are converted into reference flows and how non-functional attributes are handled. ILCD separates "obligatory properties" (binding technical and regulatory requirements) from "positioning properties" (market features such as comfort or appearance), and illustrates the conversion in Table 4 for exterior wall paint over a ten-year protection period: solvent-based Paint A (two coats, recoated after five years) requires a reference flow of 6.5 L (with footnote 39 noting old-coat removal and future coating conditions), whereas water-based Paint B (one coat lasting ten years) requires 3.8 L. EU PEF illustrates the four elements with decorative paint (protecting and decorating 1 m² of substrate for 50 years at a minimum hiding power of ≥ 98%) and adds two binding rules: the number of products needed to meet the specified service life must in principle be rounded up (unless justified otherwise), and any subjective or non-quantified attributes omitted from the functional unit must be disclosed and justified.
claims.scope: Comparison of ILCD obligatory/positioning properties and Table 4 conversion against PEF rounding-up and mandatory disclosure of uncovered attributes

claims.text: The fourth divergence concerns whether fixing a functional unit authorizes public comparative assertions. Even when two alternatives are converted to reference flows under identical four-element definitions, the permissions granted by each framework differ sharply. EU PEF (Annex I §1) allows cross-product comparisons and public comparative assertions only when the study strictly follows an applicable Product Environmental Footprint Category Rules (PEFCR) document. The GHG Protocol Product Standard states in Appendix A that, as written, it supports longitudinal performance tracking of the same product over time rather than ISO 14044 cross-product comparative assertions; comparing different products requires additional product rules, equivalent boundaries, and third-party assurance. ILCD requires comparative studies to verify consistency in scenarios, service life, maintenance, data quality, and modeling alongside functional-unit alignment.
claims.scope: Divergent admissibility gates for cross-product comparisons and public comparative assertions across PEF, GHG Protocol, and ILCD

claims.text: This comparison also marks the epistemic boundary of functional reference: standard clauses can prescribe how to formulate a functional unit, declared unit, or reference product and set admissibility gates, but they cannot substitute for empirical evidence on actual service life, aging and degradation, user behavior, or non-functional substitution preferences. Treating a calculated reference flow, rounded product count, or activity-level reference product as proof of real-world market equivalence still requires independent engineering and use-phase evidence. Furthermore, because the full texts of ISO 14040 and ISO 14044 are copyright-protected and paywalled, open-access comparisons do not quote their clauses verbatim; exact compliance requirements must be verified against licensed ISO texts. Having fixed the functional reference and reference flow, the next chapter turns to the second judgment: given how much product must be delivered, how a linear process network determines the supply activities required to deliver it.
claims.scope: Empirical limits of cross-framework functional-reference comparisons and citation boundaries for paywalled ISO standards

claims.text: The preceding chapter examined how much product is needed to deliver a given service. Once that required quantity is known, the analyst must calculate how much each supplying process in the network needs to operate. A system may deliver only a single product to the outside world while several internal processes supply one another. This chapter first establishes the basis on which each process record is expressed and then solves for the scaling factor of each process. Those scaling factors give the modeled activity levels; how real equipment operates and whether the underlying data fit the case still require separate evidence.
claims.scope: Author link between service/alternative quantities and net external demand and internal activities in a given process system; not an empirical supply-chain claim for any product
caveats: Demand coordinates and process relations belong to an explicitly specified model; formal expression does not establish real-world service equivalence, data adequacy, or supply-chain completeness.

claims.text: Inventory calculation begins with given process records. In the publicly available sample chapters of their 2002 monograph, Heijungs and Suh explain how to combine those records without addressing in that computational exposition how the numbers are measured, estimated, or collected. The opening chapters treat the given entries as deterministic quantities in order to set up the governing equations. This chapter follows the same order: given a set of process records, how do we compute results consistent with their quantitative relationships? Whether those records accurately describe a real-world system must be verified separately.
claims.scope: Computational scope stated in Chapter 1 of the Heijungs and Suh (2002) publicly available sample
caveats: Introductory sections of the publicly available sample do not establish the complete arguments of later chapters.

claims.text: Each flow is first assigned a fixed row specifying its name, unit, and direction. The Heijungs and Suh sample adopts the sign convention of negative inputs and positive outputs. Switching to another sign convention requires applying it consistently throughout; changing a unit requires rescaling the corresponding numerical values; and reordering rows requires moving flow names, units, and values together. Arranged side by side, each column represents one process. Products, materials, energy, and services exchanged between processes are economic flows and form the technology matrix A; exchanges between processes and the environment form the intervention matrix B. Both matrices share the same process columns, while each row retains its own unit.
claims.scope: Sign convention and matrix organization in §2.1 of the Heijungs and Suh (2002) sample
caveats: Other publications or software tools may use different sign conventions; identical matrix names do not guarantee identical definitions.

claims.text: Consider an author-constructed two-process example to fix these coordinates. Process 1 requires 0.5 units of Product 2 to produce 1 unit of Product 1, while Process 2 requires 0.1 units of Product 1 to produce 1 unit of Product 2; each record is normalized to one unit of output. Ordering the product rows and process columns as (1, 2) gives the technology matrix A = [[1, −0.1], [−0.5, 1]]. The system must deliver a net external demand of 1 unit of Product 1 and 0 units of Product 2, written as f = [1, 0]. Each unit record of Process 1 and Process 2 also emits 2 kg and 1 kg, respectively, of a single hypothetical substance to the environment, giving B = [2, 1]. All numbers are synthetic inputs chosen to make supply feedback transparent.
claims.scope: Author-constructed two-process model normalized to unit output with a single hypothetical elementary emission in kilograms; not a complete product study design
caveats: All coefficients are synthetic inputs; external sources support only the notation and calculation rules, not empirical validity of the hypothetical numbers.

claims.text: The next step is to solve for the scaling factor of each process, collected in the scaling vector s. The balance equation As = f multiplies each column of A by its scaling factor and sums across each row: for every product, positive outputs and negative inputs offset one another so that net delivery equals the external demand in f. In the sample's basic model, if A is square and its row equations are linearly independent, then A is nonsingular (invertible) and the unique solution is s = A⁻¹f. This formula solves the specified model; where to truncate the system, which processes and flows to include, and how to handle multifunctional processes still require prior modeling justification.
claims.scope: Basic model and unique-solution conditions in the Heijungs and Suh (2002) sample; excludes extensions outside the sample
caveats: Singular or non-square matrices may require other treatments; this paragraph does not claim that such systems never admit solutions.

claims.text: A scaling factor must always be read together with the reference basis of its process record. As Heijungs and Suh (§2.6) show, multiplying an entire process column by a positive constant c divides its scaling factor by c when external demand is held fixed. When both process records and external demand are expressed as quantities, the scaling factor is dimensionless. If process data are instead expressed as flow rates per unit time while demand remains a quantity, the scaling factor carries units of time, representing the operating duration needed at that rate to meet the demand. Without first checking how the record is normalized, a scaling factor cannot be interpreted as the number of times a piece of equipment is actually run.
claims.scope: Reference-process representation and scaling-factor interpretation in §2.6 of the Heijungs and Suh (2002) author-linked sample; flow-rate form is a conditional alternative
