caveats: Time dimensions depend on the flow-rate formulation; they do not provide actual equipment start counts, dynamic emission profiles, or empirical operating logs.

claims.text: Once the activity levels are determined, the same scaling vector multiplies the process columns of B and sums identical environmental flows to yield the inventory vector g = Bs. This step aggregates total modeled emissions and resource extractions across the listed activities, relying on linear scaling with activity level and additivity within each flow. Explaining when and where emissions occur, or whether processes scale proportionally as output changes, requires additional models; translating inventory totals into environmental consequences requires life cycle impact assessment.
claims.scope: Meaning of the basic model in the 2002 sample and applicability of its linearity and additivity assumptions
caveats: Inventory totals do not directly constitute impact assessment results or superiority judgments between alternatives.

claims.text: Applying the balance equation to the two-process example with scaling factors s₁ and s₂ yields s₁ − 0.1s₂ = 1 for Product 1 and s₂ = 0.5s₁ for Product 2. Substituting the second equation into the first gives s₁ = 20/19 and s₂ = 10/19. Aggregating through B produces total emissions of 2 × (20/19) + 10/19 = 50/19 kg, or approximately 2.632 kg. More than one unit of Process 1 is required because Process 2—which supplies Process 1—also consumes Product 1. Even though external demand for Product 2 is zero, Process 2 must operate internally, and the two scaling factors must satisfy both balances simultaneously.
claims.scope: Applies strictly to the hypothetical A, B, and f defined above under linearity and additivity assumptions
caveats: Exact rational solutions apply only to the specified model and do not verify correct implementation in any life cycle assessment (LCA) software.

claims.text: With the balance equation in place, a natural follow-up question arises: if we change how the rows are represented, does the original delivery requirement remain enforced? Holding the processes, scaling vector, and demand target fixed, suppose we rewrite the rows through a known linear mapping R, giving A′ = RA and f′ = Rf. Any activity vector satisfying As = f automatically satisfies A′s = f′. If R is invertible, the converse holds as well, so both systems permit the exact same set of activities. Converting an electricity row from megajoules (MJ) to kilowatt-hours (kWh), for example, requires rescaling both the matrix entries and the demand entry in that row—never rescaling the matrix while leaving demand in the old unit. This transforms how rows express quantities, which is distinct from rescaling a process column's reference basis, and algebraic equivalence still does not prove that the recorded service meets real-world use requirements.
claims.scope: Sufficient algebraic condition for preserving feasible activity sets under a known row mapping with fixed activity variables; does not require A itself to be invertible
caveats: Algebraic constraints in a fixed model do not substitute for evidence on service performance, data fitness, or actual supply relationships.

claims.text: Heijungs, Settanni, and Guinée (2013) illustrate this with a hypothetical chair case solving for the activities needed to deliver 1 year of sitting. In their dataset, each unit of the use process takes 5 chairs as input, delivers 10 years of sitting, and generates 5 discarded chairs. Delivering 1 year of sitting therefore sets the use activity to 0.1. Chair manufacturing (normalized to 1 chair produced) takes an activity level of 0.5, and disposal (normalized to 1 discarded chair received) likewise takes 0.5. Across the full network, these activities require 1 MJ of electricity and 2.5 kg of wood.
claims.scope: Activity levels derived for 1 year of sitting in the hypothetical chair case of Heijungs, Settanni, and Guinée (2013)
caveats: This is a linear pedagogical case constructed in the paper; sitting duration and process inputs are hypothetical data.

claims.text: The paper prices discarded chairs at −2 EUR per chair. Because each unit of the disposal process receives one discarded chair (recorded as −1 in the physical table), multiplying quantity by price should yield +2 EUR in revenue. In Eq. (10), however, that entry is printed as 20. Multiplying the printed value by the disposal activity of 0.5 produces 10 EUR in disposal revenue against the 1 EUR paid by the use process, leaving a 9 EUR discrepancy on the discarded-chair row. Recalculating from the paper's stated price–quantity relation gives 1 EUR for disposal, matching Eq. (12) and Table 3.
claims.scope: Printed disposal entry, value derived from the stated row-pricing relation, and term-by-term verification in the chair case
caveats: Text on p. 1726 states chair-manufacturing costs of 5 EUR for wood and 2.5 EUR for electricity, whereas Table 3 lists 2.5 EUR for wood and 5 EUR for electricity; both pairs sum to 7.5 EUR.
Both the printed value and the value derived from the authors' stated price–quantity and scaling relations are retained here; formal erratum status has not been verified.

claims.text: Because sitting has no market transaction in this hypothetical setup, the authors assign a price of 0 EUR per year of sitting. Multiplying both the sitting row and the 1-year final demand by zero turns the service constraint into 0 = 0. Under the correctly recalculated price–quantity matrix, both the original activity vector and the all-zero activity vector satisfy the monetary balance. Returning to the physical table, however, all-zero activities leave a residual of −1 year of sitting—delivering none of the required service.
claims.scope: Loss of the service constraint caused by zero-priced sitting under the paper's stated row-by-row pricing transformation
caveats: A zero price reflects only the absence of a market transaction for sitting in this setup; the user still purchases chairs and pays for end-of-life disposal.

claims.text: This does not mean the authors miscalculated sitting volume from a monetary equation. Heijungs, Settanni, and Guinée (2013) explicitly note that an unpriced function creates a zero row in the monetary matrix, making matrix inversion from monetary demand impossible. They therefore solve for activities in physical (natural) units first and carry those activities into cost accounting, a sequence preserved in their summary Table 6. In that way, the unpriced 1 year of sitting still governs manufacturing and disposal scale, while the monetary ledger reports the associated cash flows. In this example, the use process incurs 13.5 EUR in combined chair-purchase and disposal expenditures; pricing sitting at zero neither reduces those expenditures to zero nor implies that the service lacks utility.
claims.scope: Solution sequence in §3.5 and Table 6 and cost interpretation of the main chair case; not a verification of software behavior or real-world costs
caveats: Algebraic constraints in a fixed model do not substitute for evidence on service performance, data fitness, or actual supply relationships.

claims.text: When the original 1-year sitting equation is appended back to the monetary matrix reconstructed from the stated price–quantity relations, the original activity vector is fully recovered. Because each unit of the use process delivers 10 years of sitting, demanding 1 year fixes the use activity at 0.1; the remaining four rows all have nonzero prices, so dividing each by its unit price restores the physical balances and yields 0.5 for manufacturing and 0.5 for disposal. If the printed value of 20 is kept instead, restoring the sitting constraint yields a disposal activity of only 0.05, leaving 0.45 discarded chairs unbalanced in the physical table. Reinstating a lost service constraint and correcting an inconsistent monetary coefficient are therefore two separate repairs.
claims.scope: Recovery of original activity levels by reattaching the physical sitting equation to the stated price–quantity transformation
caveats: Recovery relies on the four monetary equations constructed from the stated price–quantity relations; keeping the printed 20 EUR in Eq. (10) yields a disposal activity of 0.05 and leaves 0.45 discarded chairs unbalanced.

claims.text: To judge whether a row transformation relaxes the original requirement, one asks whether it accepts activities that previously failed to balance. With the feasible activity set and final demand fixed, the residual of any activity vector is its supply minus demand. Applying the same linear row mapping to supply and demand always preserves existing solutions. The transformed system has the exact same solution set if and only if no nonzero residual produced by an admissible activity vector is mapped to zero. Any invertible mapping satisfies this condition, yet a non-invertible mapping can also preserve the solution set when the remaining constraints are already sufficient—for instance, when a completely redundant balance row is dropped.
claims.scope: Necessary and sufficient condition for a linear row mapping to preserve the solution set given a fixed activity set, balance relation, and final demand
caveats: This condition compares only numerical balances of admissible activities within a fixed model; real-world service performance and use conditions still require separate verification.

claims.text: Dropping a row does not always alter the solution. Suppose a model has a single activity, where Row 1 requires delivering 1 unit and Row 2 multiplies both sides of that same supply–demand balance by 2. Replacing Row 2 with 0 = 0 cannot be reversed by an invertible matrix, yet the unique solution remains an activity level of 1 because satisfying Row 1 automatically satisfies Row 2.
claims.scope: Monograph-constructed single-activity contrast showing that removing a redundant balance row leaves the solution unchanged
caveats: Row 2 duplicates the exact scalar multiple of Row 1, including the demand side.

claims.text: Choosing between physical (natural) units and monetary units therefore depends on which requirement the study must preserve. Natural units in the paper encompass not only mass, but also energy, counts, and time—and some services may indeed be defined in monetary terms. When a study aims to estimate supply activities driven by a known procurement expenditure, monetary demand directly expresses the research question. Treating a monetary demand as equivalent to another service demand, however, requires stating the mapping conditions and verifying that no previously inadmissible activity is allowed through. In the chair case, a zero-priced row erased the sitting-scale constraint; in the feedback example below, the original equations remain intact, but mutual supply is left unresolved. The two omissions require different remedies.
claims.scope: Constraint preservation and research-question selection in fixed models; does not dismiss monetary analysis in general or verify real-world service performance
caveats: Algebraic constraints in a fixed model do not substitute for evidence on service performance, data fitness, or actual supply relationships.

claims.text: Tracing only one upstream tier in the two-process example records 1 unit of Process 1 and the 0.5 units of Process 2 it directly requires, giving emissions of 2 + 0.5 = 2.5 kg. Substituting [1, 0.5] back into the original matrix A exposes the shortfall: net delivery is only [0.95, 0], leaving Product 1 short by 0.05 units because Process 2's own requirement for Product 1 was omitted. For this synthetic dataset, 2.5 kg sits exactly 5% below the full balance solution of 50/19 kg. That 5% gap measures only the truncation of this constructed example; real-world inventory truncation error must be estimated separately.
claims.scope: Same synthetic model; comparison between a one-tier expansion and the full two-process balance solution
caveats: 5% is not an empirical error rate and cannot be used as a general correction factor for real inventories.

claims.text: Two kinds of omission must be kept distinct. When both Process 1 and Process 2 are already in the model and only the feedback from Process 2 back to Process 1 was skipped, solving the simultaneous balance equations captures both internal demands completely. When a process was never included in the model in the first place, solving the equations cannot conjure it back. As Suh and co-authors emphasize in discussing system boundaries, matrix inversion resolves upstream links only among processes already inside the modeled boundary. The next chapter returns to process records to examine how a given input or waste-treatment requirement is linked to the supplying or treating process actually represented in a database.
claims.scope: Limited interpretation drawn from the synthetic calculation and cited methodological passages; not a general error estimate
caveats: Solving a given balance system does not establish that the real-world system is completely represented, that functions are equivalent, or that environmental conclusions are valid.

claims.text: When a factory sends wastewater past its gate, the stream has left the facility without necessarily entering a natural water body. If the wastewater travels to a treatment plant, leaving the factory gate crosses an interface between two technical processes; only the pollutants discharged into a river after treatment cross the boundary between the technical system and the environment. Defining a system boundary therefore requires separating two distinct questions: which processes the study includes, and which exchanges the model treats as direct exchanges with the environment. The first question determines how far the study traces the supply and disposal chain; the second determines what enters the environmental inventory.
claims.scope: Bounded synthesis of boundary provisions read in ISO 2006, CML 2001, and ILCD 2010
caveats: The factory-gate example illustrates the two types of boundaries and does not represent an empirical emissions survey of any real facility.

claims.text: International Organization for Standardization (ISO) standard ISO 14040:2006 defines an elementary flow as material or energy drawn directly from the environment without previous human transformation, or released directly into the environment without subsequent human transformation. Even when different frameworks or software manuals share the label "elementary flow", the shared label does not guarantee identical classification criteria; each system's boundary rules must still be verified. Product systems may also exchange product flows with other product systems; the standard does not classify every flow crossing a study boundary as an elementary flow. ISO 14044:2006 permits omitting inputs, outputs, or unit processes only if they do not significantly change the overall conclusions of the study, and requires stating the criteria and effect of exclusions and cut-offs. Failing to link wastewater treatment because data are unavailable leaves an open technical gap in the model—it does not justify relabeling the entire wastewater stream as a specific pollutant already discharged into a river.
claims.scope: Definitions and scope clauses listed in the public preview of the ISO 14040/14044:2006 base editions
caveats: Only the specified original clauses of the 2006 base editions were inspected; this does not represent a review of the full standards, subsequent amendments, or current consolidated editions.

claims.text: Even after separating those two questions, different methodological frameworks do not draw the environmental interface in the same place. For unmanaged landfills, the 2001 operational guide from the Institute of Environmental Sciences, Leiden University (CML) treats the landfill itself as part of the environment, allowing the bulk waste stream entering it to be recorded as an emission. By contrast, the 2010 International Reference Life Cycle Data System (ILCD) Handbook requires modeling the release of specific substances and related environmental interventions from the waste. That rule extends even to a battery discarded in nature: although the battery physically lies in the environment, the model retains it on the technical side and tracks the substances it releases into soil, water, and air. Both guides thus place the inventory interface at different points for the same physical situation.
claims.scope: Comparison of unmanaged disposal in CML 2001 Part 3 §3.2 and ILCD 2010 §§6.6.1 and 7.4.4.2
caveats: Unmanaged disposal rules are not generalized to all controlled landfills; both guides specify finer conditions and exceptions.

claims.text: That boundary difference changes the object that impact characterization receives. Kilograms of bulk waste cannot directly substitute for kilograms of a specific metal leached into water; which characterization factor applies depends on the exact substance and environmental compartment from which the factor begins. ILCD disaggregates complex waste streams so that inventory flows connect cleanly to corresponding impact models, yet composition, release pathways, and time horizons still require evidence. CML likewise discusses long-term emissions and temporal assumptions. Being more disaggregated or published later does not by itself prove that one guide predicts emissions from a real landfill more accurately than the other.
claims.scope: Object differences and conditional consequences across the two inspected guides
caveats: No field observations were used to validate the numerical accuracy of either modeling interface for a given site.

claims.text: Divergences on agricultural land likewise stem from where each model draws the process boundary. The CML 2001 guide places agricultural activities inside the economic system while leaving natural soil on the environmental side, and discusses pesticide emissions after subtracting the fraction removed with the harvested crop; horticulture on artificial substrates is treated differently, and the guide allows other consistent boundary choices to be discussed. The ILCD 2010 Handbook generally places managed agricultural land on the technical side and distinguishes the applied amount from environmental interventions such as spray drift, volatilization, runoff, and leaching. Amounts applied to a field, removed with the harvest, and entering water bodies therefore cannot substitute for one another simply because all three are measured in kilograms.
claims.scope: Comparison of the CML 2001 natural-soil boundary and the ILCD 2010 managed-land boundary
caveats: Agricultural provisions retain conditions on baselines, crop or land functions, and persistent substances; no empirical field emission factors are provided here.

claims.text: The environmental interface is therefore a conditional modeling rule rather than a blanket slogan. For certain heavy metals and persistent organic pollutants remaining long-term in soil, ILCD separately requires recording emissions to soil while avoiding double counting with erosion transfers; it also specifies dedicated rules for radioactive waste, underground disposal, and qualifying aggregate indicators. Where the chosen impact method covers physical interventions caused by litter, those interventions must also be recorded. Consequently, "managed land belongs to the technical system" cannot be compressed into "agricultural land has no soil emissions", nor can "model through to environmental interventions" be compressed into "every inventory record must be a single chemical substance".
claims.scope: Specified agricultural, waste, and aggregate-indicator exceptions in ILCD 2010
caveats: This explains only the rules and exceptions in the cited historical guidance and does not claim to cover every class of environmental intervention.

claims.text: Once concepts enter data files, one must also separate the defined object from a concrete transfer into or out of a process. ILCD Format 1.1 uses a Flow data set to define a flow's identity and measurement properties—along with compartment categorization for elementary flows—and separately references it via an exchange inside a Process data set to record direction and amount for that process. The same flow can appear in exchanges across multiple processes or multiple times within a single process. The flow's default measurement property (such as mass) specifies what physical quantity measures it; a given exchange's amount specifies how much enters or leaves in that process record. An object definition does not predetermine the quantity or role of any individual exchange.
claims.scope: Original Flow and Process data set fields in ILCD Format 1.1
caveats: Format field capabilities do not prove how actual software preserves links, resolves versions, or executes calculations.

claims.text: First identify the object sitting on the arrow. The openLCA 2 manual divides flows into three types: elementary flows, product flows, and waste flows. Material or energy drawn from the natural environment without previous human transformation—such as extracted crude oil—can be recorded as an elementary flow, as can material or energy released into the environment without subsequent human transformation, such as emissions to air. Product flows and waste flows must be identified in light of their role in a process; the manual notes that waste paper sent for recycling can also be modeled as a product flow.
claims.scope: Flow data objects in the openLCA 2 manual
caveats: This cannot be treated as a mutually exclusive classification shared by all LCA standards.

claims.text: Whenever a process uses or generates a flow, it requires a separate exchange entry. In openLCA's Inputs/Outputs table, each exchange references a defined flow and specifies its amount, unit, and direction as an input or output. A single defined flow can be referenced by many exchanges across many processes.
claims.scope: Process editor in openLCA 2

claims.text: Water makes this two-layer distinction concrete. The flow definition specifies what kind of object water is; the exchange records how much water a given factory uses, in what unit, and on which side of the process. Even when two factories reference the exact same flow object, each retains its own exchange quantity and role. When auditing an inventory, identify the flow object first and then return to the specific exchange in which it occurs.
claims.scope: Analytical distinction between flows and process inputs/outputs in openLCA
caveats: This is an analytical distinction and is not claimed to be a uniform terminological definition adopted by all standards.

claims.text: ISO's conceptual terms for elementary flows and product systems, ILCD Format 1.1 flow data sets, and flows referenced by exchanges in openLCA operate at different layers. Conditional mappings can be built across them, but shared names do not permit blind field-by-field substitution. For instance, ILCD Format 1.1 also includes an "Other flow" type, whereas the openLCA 2 manual presents three flow types here. A different number of enumerated categories reflects representational scope rather than competing theories of natural processes; any concrete conversion must still verify the exchanged object, its role, and its links.
claims.scope: Comparison of normative terminology with ILCD Format 1.1 and openLCA 2 data-representation layers
caveats: No cross-software conversion experiment was performed for ILCD Other flow records.

claims.text: Two records with the same name and unit can still represent different environmental flows. In the Environmental Footprint (EF) 3.1 reference package, two elementary flows both named "aluminium (iii)" are measured by mass with the reference unit kg, yet one refers to agricultural soil and the other to long-term unspecified water, with distinct data set identities. In the inspected freshwater ecotoxicity method, the two flows correspond to a positive factor and a zero entry respectively; one cannot merge them by name first and then pick either factor arbitrarily. Agricultural soil also contains a separate record named "aluminium" whose factor happens to match the agricultural-soil "aluminium (iii)" entry, but that numerical match does not make the two identities interchangeable in other methods or uses. Distinct identities may still be aggregated for an explicit purpose, provided the preserved quantity, composition, and mapping basis are documented.
claims.scope: Selected official EF 3.1 flows, mass property and unit definitions, and freshwater ecotoxicity method entries
caveats: Only selected members of the official package were inspected; full mappings, underlying factor-calculation routines, and environmental effects were not verified. The reason for the zero entry in long-term water remains undetermined.

claims.text: A flow's identity also depends on the question being asked. ISO 14040:2006 defines waste as substances or objects that the holder intends or is required to dispose of, whereas the CML 2001 guide defines economic flows to encompass exchanges of positive, zero, or negative value, distinguishing waste for treatment from products within that context. Residual economic value alone does not settle whether an object requires disposal, and a software label of "product" does not by itself tell whether a model includes end-of-life treatment. Disposal status, traded commodity, and software flow type must each be stated separately.
claims.scope: Bounded comparison of ISO 2006 definitions, CML 2001 terminology, and native software type observations
caveats: This does not determine the legal waste classification of any specific material and does not treat historical economic-value classifications as a universal rule across all databases.

claims.text: The direction of physical material movement and the direction of a purchased service can also diverge. When a factory hands waste to a treatment facility, it simultaneously receives a disposal service; even if that service is measured per kilogram of material treated, it does not become a physical commodity traveling in the same direction. Analyzing such exchanges through the functions that processes supply or use, Suh demonstrates that physical dimensions and net monetary payments alone cannot identify the function of an exchange. The ILCD 2010 Handbook accordingly allows accounting either as a waste output or as a treatment-service input, while recommending the material-flow direction to facilitate mass and elemental balances. That conceptual correspondence is not yet a software sign convention.
claims.scope: Conditional correspondence between Suh (2004, dissertation Chapter III) and ILCD 2010 treatment-direction rules
caveats: Services measured in the same physical unit do not guarantee identical composition, facility, or environmental consequences; a handbook's service representation does not automatically equal openLCA's negative-product encoding.

claims.text: Sending a batch of waste from a factory to a treatment facility takes only a single arrow on paper. To compute how much the facility treats, software must also know which processes sit at each end, how much is sent, and what reference quantity scales the treatment record. A file import may display the waste flow intact while the solver silently omits the treatment process. The bottle and injection-molding examples below trace how treatment enters calculation, and then examine which results change—and why—when the same model moves across file formats or characterization factors.
claims.scope: How an exchange demands another activity; named cases using pinned source files and openLCA 2.7.0 native modules

claims.text: Identifying an input or output still leaves open who supplies or treats it. An openLCA product system stores the link between a specific exchange and its chosen provider separately. Although an exchange may also carry a default provider field, determining which supplying process the solver will actually invoke requires checking the links saved in the product system rather than trusting the name in the default field.
claims.scope: How an exchange demands another activity; named cases using pinned source files and openLCA 2.7.0 native modules

claims.text: Once a supplying process is selected, calculation must determine how many multiples of its record are needed. A process's quantitative reference gives the input or output amount represented by one unit of that record. The product system's target amount is taken up by the reference process, while each linked supplying or treatment process takes up the demand issued by the exchange connected to it. When a process has a single reference flow and scales proportionally, dividing the demand placed on that process by its reference amount yields the activity scaling factor needed to meet that demand. Before dividing, measurement units must be harmonized and input/output direction and sign conventions applied; if the reference exchange contains a formula, it must first be evaluated under the active parameters. That scaling factor is relative to the model record's reference basis—determining how many times real equipment actually ran requires operational records.
claims.scope: How an exchange demands another activity; named cases using pinned source files and openLCA 2.7.0 native modules

claims.text: For modeling waste treatment, the openLCA manual describes a convention aligned with physical movement called "material flow logic". The waste-generating process records a waste output, while the treatment process records a waste input and designates that input as its quantitative reference. When reading a treatment record under this convention, look for the reference amount on the input side.
claims.scope: Material flow logic as described in the openLCA 2 manual

claims.text: GreenDelta's bottle tutorial provides a controlled side-by-side test of both conventions. The tutorial targets openLCA 1.10; here, the archived database backup is restored into a working copy, migrated, and solved with the official openLCA 2.7.0 Java modules. The findings below describe the calculation behavior of that pinned teaching model in that module version. The tutorial text and archived database can be inspected independently; how a historical desktop patch behaved at release, or what environmental performance real bottles achieve, requires separate evidence.
claims.scope: How an exchange demands another activity; named cases using pinned source files and openLCA 2.7.0 native modules
caveats: This case uses JavaSolver and pinned dependencies; the original database and full re-exports are not redistributed with the public summary.

claims.text: The bottle use process takes 1.06500 kg of filled water bottle as input, designates 0.06500 kg of "PET Bottle, disposed" (polyethylene terephthalate) as its product-output quantitative reference, and uses a second exchange referencing a different flow object to link to incineration. The reference output sets how much bottle mass the calculation represents, while the treatment exchange demands incineration of that same mass of discarded material, with its flow type and direction determined by whichever of the two conventions is used. Because those two records represent the calculation basis and the treatment demand for the same batch of bottles, their masses cannot be added together. Nor does the tutorial's exchange table fully account for the final fate of the drinking water.
claims.scope: How an exchange demands another activity; named cases using pinned source files and openLCA 2.7.0 native modules

claims.text: Under material flow logic, the use process records an output of 0.06500 kg of a waste flow, and the treatment process uses an input of 1000.00000 kg as its reference. Both recorded quantities are positive, yet one unit of the use record generates far less waste than the treatment record's reference basis. Scaling the treatment activity along the link therefore requires converting between those two quantities.
claims.scope: Two encodings of the same treatment quantity; named cases using pinned source files and openLCA 2.7.0 native modules

claims.text: The openLCA manual also describes an "opposite direction approach". Here the flow type is changed to "product", the waste-generating process records a negative input, and the treatment process records a negative output. Physical material still moves from generator to treatment facility; the software encodes that direction through the combination of flow type, input/output side, and sign.
claims.scope: Opposite direction approach as described in the openLCA 2 manual

claims.text: The same batch of bottles can be encoded in the opposite direction. The use process records a product input of −0.06500 kg, and the treatment process takes a product output of −1000.00000 kg as its reference. The minus sign must be read together with the input/output side at both ends to identify which process demands treatment; the physical mass of the bottles remains positive.
claims.scope: Two encodings of the same treatment quantity; named cases using pinned source files and openLCA 2.7.0 native modules

claims.text: Both reference quantities are now fixed. Setting the product system target to 0.06500 kg of reference bottle requires exactly one unit of the use record. The linked treatment activity scaling factor is 0.06500 ÷ 1000.00000 = 0.000065; dividing the two negative quantities in the opposite-direction encoding yields the exact same positive scaling factor. Both encodings demand the same amount of treatment here because reference, quantity, and link are matched item for item.
claims.scope: Two encodings of the same treatment quantity; named cases using pinned source files and openLCA 2.7.0 native modules

claims.text: Next examine how both encodings enter the balance equation. When the treatment reference and the use process's treatment exchange are assembled into the technology matrix in this case, outputs enter with their recorded sign while inputs are negated. Consequently, both the positive 1000 kg waste input and the negative 1000 kg product output produce −1000, while both the positive 0.065 kg waste output and the negative 0.065 kg product input produce +0.065. The treatment diagonal entry and off-diagonal link entry are thus identical across both unallocated models. With one unit of the use record, the treatment balance reads 0.065 − 1000 × treatment scaling factor = 0. The negative diagonal entry offsets the generated waste mass; it does not mean the facility treats negative mass.
claims.scope: Two encodings of the same treatment quantity; named cases using pinned source files and openLCA 2.7.0 native modules

claims.text: To compare two sets of records reliably, first sketch where the physical material comes from and where it goes, then align flow type, process roles at both ends, input/output side, sign, and quantitative reference. Reading minus signs in isolation mistakes a computational sign convention for a definition of waste; reading the "product" label in isolation hides the fact that the material is awaiting disposal. Checking all of these fields clarifies this example, while other software systems require inspecting their own conventions.
claims.scope: Reading and comparing the two waste-modeling conventions above
caveats: The existence of two modeling conventions does not prove that any two models can be converted losslessly into one another.

claims.text: Switching software to Brightway requires re-checking sign conventions from scratch. Brightway's documentation places process-to-product supply-chain relations in the technosphere matrix and exchanges between processes and the natural environment in a separate matrix. Positive technosphere values represent production and negative values represent consumption. Because a process can output waste without waste generation being the purpose of the process, identifying which edge carries the functional role still requires checking Brightway's node and edge conventions.
claims.scope: Technosphere matrix conventions in Brightway latest documentation

claims.text: In Brightway, the "input" and "output" fields specify how product or biosphere nodes connect to process nodes within its graph schema. Interpreting which way physical material moves requires knowing that schema's definitions; sharing the same English words with another software tool does not allow transferring that tool's direction rules.
claims.scope: Important callout box in Brightway latest Matrix Construction documentation
caveats: This reflects the conventions stated in the cited documentation; the behavior of any specific installed version must be verified against that version.

claims.text: Even when activity levels are identical, impact scores can diverge if allocation settings differ. The tutorial's incineration process involves waste treatment alongside electricity and steam outputs; allocation determines what share of the process's burden each function carries, with economic allocation deriving shares from quantities, costs, and revenues. In the archived database, the material-flow-logic treatment process defaults to economic allocation, whereas the opposite-direction process does not carry the same setting. To avoid conflating burden partitioning with representational equivalence, the encoding comparison here explicitly fixes allocation to none (NONE), while evaluating economic allocation separately.
claims.scope: Two encodings of the same treatment quantity; named cases using pinned source files and openLCA 2.7.0 native modules

claims.text: To isolate the two encodings, target demand, background data, links, and the no-allocation setting are held constant. Once the two pairs of use processes, treatment processes, and treatment flows are matched by role, the technology supply-demand matrix, the per-unit inventory matrix, and the flow-to-impact characterization matrix are identical. Both runs contain 10 activity coordinates, 435 inventory coordinates, and 11 impact categories, with totals matching within floating-point tolerance. For example, 100-year global warming potential (GWP100a) is approximately 0.369674399 kg CO₂ eq (kilograms of carbon dioxide equivalent) in both runs. Both the matrix correspondence and the score agreement remain strictly bounded to this coordinate set and configuration.
claims.scope: Two encodings of the same treatment quantity; named cases using pinned source files and openLCA 2.7.0 native modules
caveats: Pairing is explicitly restricted to these two named models; minor floating-point summation-order differences occur in inventory and category totals, and byte-for-byte output identity is not claimed.

claims.text: Outside openLCA's two field encodings, the bottle quantities can also be written on paper using a service-direction balance. Let U be the use-activity scaling factor and H be the treatment-activity scaling factor: the use process inputs a disposal service measured by 0.065 kg of waste treated, and one unit of the treatment facility outputs the same service measured by 1000 kg of waste treated, giving the service balance −0.065U + 1000H = 0. Here kg measures the mass of waste treated by the service, not a physical mass carried by the service itself. Written in the material direction, the balance is 0.065U − 1000H = 0; at U = 1, both equations yield H = 0.000065. If the same row also carries an external delivery or absorption demand, reversing direction requires negating the right-hand side as well. This author derivation does not execute a new service model and is not the same thing as openLCA's negative-product fields above: the conceptual direction of a service flow and how software interprets flow type, side, and sign must be verified separately. Whenever the facility, waste composition, linking, or allocation changes, multiplying a row by −1 no longer establishes equivalence.
claims.scope: Author's algebraic derivation on the fixed bottle reference quantities, distinct from native software runs
caveats: No new software run was executed here; negating a balance row for a service direction is a different argument from two native field encodings assembling into the same matrix.

claims.text: To verify directly that incineration participated in the calculation, check a specific substance emitted to freshwater by the treatment process. In the tutorial figure, the treatment record—referenced to 1000 kg of waste—emits 0.00000000101665 kg of Acenaphthene to freshwater. Multiplying by the bottle's treatment scaling factor gives 6.608225e-14 kg. Because the migrated archive retains additional decimal digits in its emission coefficient, the native calculation reports a treatment-process contribution of approximately 6.608199e-14 kg. The two values agree within the precision shown in the tutorial figure; this check verifies only that single process's contribution to that freshwater emission flow.
claims.scope: Process contribution, single-flow total, and category total; named cases using pinned source files and openLCA 2.7.0 native modules

claims.text: Other processes in the background system also emit that same freshwater Acenaphthene flow. Including their contributions brings the system-wide inventory total for that flow to approximately 1.789707e-13 kg. That system total and the scaled treatment contribution above answer questions of different scope. Any numerical comparison must identify the exact process, flow, emission compartment, and aggregation scope so that two differently scoped numbers are not mistaken for contradictory outputs from the same run.
claims.scope: Process contribution, single-flow total, and category total; named cases using pinned source files and openLCA 2.7.0 native modules

claims.text: Carbon dioxide (CO₂) extends this distinction from inventory to impact indicator. For the selected CO₂ emission-to-air flow, the treatment process contributes approximately 0.157428377 kg, while the system-wide inventory total for that same flow is approximately 0.336530863 kg. Although the archived CML GWP100a method assigns that flow a characterization factor of 1 kg CO₂ eq per kg emitted, other characterized greenhouse gases also enter the category, bringing the category total to 0.369674399 kg CO₂ eq. Even when a characterization factor equals 1, a process contribution, a single-flow inventory total, and a category total remain three distinct quantities.
claims.scope: Process contribution, single-flow total, and category total; named cases using pinned source files and openLCA 2.7.0 native modules

claims.text: Once process contributions, inventory totals, and category totals are separated, vary only the allocation setting. Under the archived project's economic allocation, the material-flow-logic model yields a GWP100a score of approximately 0.265341691 kg CO₂ eq, compared with approximately 0.369674399 kg CO₂ eq without allocation; both match the values stored in the archived report within verification tolerance. The treatment scaling factor itself does not change—only the share of burden assigned to the reference function changes. A lower score therefore does not prove that less waste was treated or that co-produced electricity and steam displaced other activities in reality.
claims.scope: Process contribution, single-flow total, and category total; named cases using pinned source files and openLCA 2.7.0 native modules

claims.text: Screenshots printed in the tutorial support only a narrower check of displayed digits. The tutorial pane displays GWP100a as 0.36967 kg CO₂ eq and acidification as 0.00100 kg SO₂ eq (kilograms of sulfur dioxide equivalent), matching the modern unallocated calculation to the displayed precision. However, the figure caption reads "Production" while the pane title reads "Usage", the screenshot omits the full target and allocation settings, and a second allocation-project figure carries a different project identity from the archived project. Agreement at displayed rounding precision does not justify merging those materials into a single historical run.
claims.scope: Process contribution, single-flow total, and category total; named cases using pinned source files and openLCA 2.7.0 native modules

claims.text: If the treatment link is actually severed while the default provider remains populated, does the solver recover the treatment process? In a copy of the same bottle model, deleting only the single saved link from use to treatment—while keeping the waste exchange and its default provider intact and without re-linking—causes the treatment process to disappear from the solved activity index, leaving 0.065 kg of waste stranded at the unlinked boundary. The result table still lists that 0.065 kg with type WASTE_FLOW; it is an open technical flow, and its appearance in the inventory table does not turn it into an elementary flow emitted directly to nature.
claims.scope: Treatment can still be omitted even when a default provider is present; named cases using pinned source files and openLCA 2.7.0 native modules

claims.text: No treatment activity was solved in that run. Removing the link lowers GWP100a to approximately 0.212105058 kg CO₂ eq, and at the inventory level the treatment process's freshwater Acenaphthene and CO₂ contributions drop out. Both the category total and the process-level inventory change for a single, explicit modeling reason: the treatment activity is absent. The retained default provider name did not restore the activity; reading only the headline score could mistake an omitted burden for a genuine improvement in waste treatment.
claims.scope: Treatment can still be omitted even when a default provider is present; named cases using pinned source files and openLCA 2.7.0 native modules

claims.text: While the bottle example shows whether a link triggers treatment, the Joint Research Centre (JRC) extended International Reference Life Cycle Data System (eILCD) software development kit (SDK) injection-molding example tests process instances and parameters as well. The source model explicitly defines 5 parts at 0.2 kg each, totaling 1 kg. Its metadata restrict it to non-commercial import/export interface testing and exclude real life cycle assessment (LCA) studies, making it suitable for testing how model relationships transfer rather than serving as empirical data for the injection-molding industry.
claims.scope: One kilogram does not specify how many parts; named cases using pinned source files and openLCA 2.7.0 native modules

claims.text: The seven process instances in the source model reference six distinct process universally unique identifiers (UUIDs): two electricity instances point to the same grid data set, one serving rail transport and the other serving injection molding and washing. In the source file, those two instances carry their own connections, groupings, and scaling factors. Ordinary import merges both electricity demands onto a single provider. The source model preserves the distinction between the two instances, whereas the imported calculation graph uses one shared coordinate; whether other UUID-sharing instances can be merged equivalently depends on their individual roles and connections.
claims.scope: One kilogram does not specify how many parts; named cases using pinned source files and openLCA 2.7.0 native modules

claims.text: Four connections also bridge mismatched flow objects across their two ends, using different flow UUIDs such as cargo before and after transport or the required plastic granulate. The ordinary openLCA importer inserts a connector process for each of those four links, recording a quantity of 1 in each end's reference unit: three kg-to-kg bridges and one MJ-to-MJ electricity bridge. Import warnings flag these bridges and cannot be dropped from interpretation, nor can a 1:1 bridge here be generalized to arbitrary same-named flows, different units, or materials of differing mass.
claims.scope: One kilogram does not specify how many parts; named cases using pinned source files and openLCA 2.7.0 native modules

claims.text: After import, the product system target reads simply 1 kg; knowing how many parts that represents requires knowing the mass per part. The saved Baseline parameter set stores override values for part mass, rail distance, and rail utilization, while the reference output still uses a formula evaluated from part mass. Explicitly applying that parameter set divides the 1 kg target by 0.2 kg per reference activity, yielding 5 model activity units. The system target alone cannot supply that multiplier—it is recomputed from the formula, and whether the source instances' groupings and scaling factors transferred verbatim still requires separate verification.
claims.scope: One kilogram does not specify how many parts; named cases using pinned source files and openLCA 2.7.0 native modules

claims.text: A controlled test isolates the effect of part mass. Changing the mass per part to 1 kg while keeping the delivered target at 1 kg and retaining the rail parameter overrides reduces the required molding activity to 1 unit. Because the source electricity formula contains a fixed term that does not scale proportionally with part mass, delivering the same total mass of plastic no longer requires the same electricity. In this author-controlled comparison, fossil CO₂ inventory drops by approximately 0.064471482 kg relative to the five-part case; this exposes the piece-count effect built into the formula rather than measuring emissions from a real factory changing product designs.
claims.scope: One kilogram does not specify how many parts; named cases using pinned source files and openLCA 2.7.0 native modules

claims.text: One must also check whether the solver actually loads the saved parameters. In this version of openLCA, CalculationSetup.of reads the product system's target amount but does not automatically apply parameter sets saved in the system. The runs above pass Baseline explicitly; omitting all parameter overrides alters the rail parameters as well, confounding the comparison with a second change. Isolating the effect of part mass requires holding all other parameters at their original values.
claims.scope: One kilogram does not specify how many parts; named cases using pinned source files and openLCA 2.7.0 native modules

claims.text: Tracing the end-of-life injection-molding machine along its source connection reveals who actually demands activity from whom. The source example classifies the end-of-life machine as a Product flow: the molding process outputs it, and the end-of-life treatment process takes it as a positive input serving as the treatment reference. Ordinary import preserves the Product flow type and treats the product-output side as the provider. As imported, the link therefore means "end-of-life treatment draws the discarded machine from injection molding". Starting from the demanded molded parts, injection molding does not pull downstream treatment across that product-supply edge. Even when a link resolves cleanly, the actual direction of demand must be read from provider and recipient roles.
claims.scope: Treatment can still be omitted even when links are preserved; named cases using pinned source files and openLCA 2.7.0 native modules

claims.text: In the solved activity index, an extra molding coordinate appears with the end-of-life machine as output, yet no activity coordinate exists for end-of-life treatment. Approximately 4.000000e-6 kg of end-of-life machine remains in the open inventory as a PRODUCT_FLOW. The solver computes activities for the graph it receives, while the omitted end-of-life treatment stays outside the result.
claims.scope: Treatment can still be omitted even when links are preserved; named cases using pinned source files and openLCA 2.7.0 native modules

claims.text: Two gas inventories confirm the missing treatment. The source model's designated resulting process reports 1.8919649886152838 kg of fossil CO₂ in its resultingAmount field, whereas the imported graph yields approximately 1.891961100 kg; subtracting the unrounded values retained by the program—rather than the rounded display values shown here—leaves a shortfall of approximately 3.888308e-6 kg. Multiplying the unlinked end-of-life machine mass by the source treatment coefficient of 0.972076908272198 kg CO₂/kg gives approximately 3.888308e-6 kg, and the shortfall in fossil carbon monoxide (CO) likewise matches that treatment contribution. Explaining the shortfall does not insert treatment into the imported graph; the native output still lacks that contribution and does not fully reproduce the source file's two gas totals.
claims.scope: Treatment can still be omitted even when links are preserved; named cases using pinned source files and openLCA 2.7.0 native modules

claims.text: Checking only quantities unaffected by end-of-life treatment can hide this omission. Primary energy from hydropower, for instance, computes to approximately 62.286789763 MJ in the native run—matching the source file's designated result—simply because the omitted machine-treatment process has no hydropower input. Auditing only that resource flow, or rounding CO₂ to two decimal places, would mask the discrepancy in both gas inventories. Verifying whether key processes entered the calculation requires selecting quantities sensitive to those processes.
claims.scope: Treatment can still be omitted even when links are preserved; named cases using pinned source files and openLCA 2.7.0 native modules

claims.text: After checking those two gases, inspect what the source file's designated result actually lists. Under the source relations, washing generates approximately 0.019400 kg of unlinked plastic waste, which the native inventory preserves, whereas the seven exchanges of the designated resulting process omit it. Moreover, all six non-reference exchanges in that resulting file report differing meanAmount and resultingAmount values despite having no variable reference, whereas ILCD documentation specifies that resultingAmount equals meanAmount multiplied by the referenced variable and should equal meanAmount when no variable is referenced. The comparison here uses the source file's recorded resultingAmount and leaves that discrepancy visible; one cannot treat a file as a benchmark while silently patching or completing it.
claims.scope: Treatment can still be omitted even when links are preserved; named cases using pinned source files and openLCA 2.7.0 native modules

claims.text: The same example also surfaces a separate versioning issue. The source electricity flow requests flow property version 28.00.000, whereas the file resolved at its Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) carries version 03.00.000. Matching UUIDs allow the importer to locate a usable record, but verifying whether the requested version was actually satisfied requires checking the version metadata directly—an identical energy total cannot answer that question.
claims.scope: Treatment can still be omitted even when links are preserved; named cases using pinned source files and openLCA 2.7.0 native modules

claims.text: Why must model conversions still check the system target? Because "reference" operates at several distinct levels. The functional unit defines the required performance; the reference flow translates that requirement into the output quantity of a specific process. A data set's quantitative reference states the basis quantity of that record, and ILCD Format 1.1 also permits functional units, other parameters, or production periods as reference types. A flow data set's reference flow property specifies the default physical quantity—such as mass or energy—used to measure the flow. Although these levels connect, the numeric value of a single reference exchange cannot automatically stand in for the full quantity and performance required by a study.
claims.scope: Reference hierarchy across ISO 14044:2006 §4.2.3.2, ILCD 2010, and ILCD Format 1.1
caveats: Conceptual alignment across reference levels does not prove that a given export format carries an independent product-system target.

claims.text: Rescaling an accounting basis must also be separated from changing the study's external demand. In a fixed linear model As = f and g = Bs, s is the vector of process scaling factors, f is the external demand vector, and g is the environmental inventory. Rescaling every process column's technical and environmental coefficients to a new basis via an invertible positive diagonal matrix D gives A′ = AD and B′ = BD; under the same demand f, the new scaling vector is s′ = D⁻¹s, and the inventory remains B′s′ = Bs. Activity multipliers change, while the inventory does not. That invariance requires checking the entire column alongside the demand vector; dropping the independent target and substituting one record's reference basis as the new demand changes how much the model is being asked to deliver.
claims.scope: Author's basis-transformation derivation within the Heijungs–Suh fixed linear model
caveats: Validity requires the same proportionally scalable linear model and an invertible positive basis transformation; it does not establish unconditional linearity of real production or general conversion equivalence.

claims.text: Knowing which activities belong to the original graph raises the next question: after exporting a model and importing it back, does the system still deliver the originally requested quantity? Answering requires stating the format, reader/writer implementation, and calculation setup. Both round-trips of the bottle model use the same openLCA version: JavaScript Object Notation for Linked Data (JSON-LD) exports the product system, its dependencies, and the original CML method, whereas eILCD exports the product system and dependencies while retaining openLCA extensions written by the exporter. Because the CML method was not selected for the eILCD export, the eILCD round-trip compares only inventories and does not test whether eILCD preserves impact-method data.
claims.scope: Which question a file round-trip preserves; named cases using pinned source files and openLCA 2.7.0 native modules

claims.text: The openLCA 2 manual notes that material flow logic for waste modeling was introduced in openLCA 1.7, whereas earlier releases used the opposite direction approach. That milestone dates the convention's introduction as recounted in the manual; determining how a legacy database migrates and solves in a given release still requires checking that migration's logs and calculation behavior.
claims.scope: Software version history as recounted in the openLCA 2 manual
caveats: Version history relies on the manual's own account and does not prove that openLCA originated the underlying concept.

claims.text: Start by testing both round-trips with the original 0.065 kg system target. Both paths preserve the inspected process identities, versions, units, and all 9 saved links, and signed inventories match under their respective targets; JSON-LD also reproduces the compared CML category results. Because the 0.065 kg system target happens to equal the reference exchange amount here, this first test cannot yet reveal whether a format carries an independently set system target.
claims.scope: Which question a file round-trip preserves; named cases using pinned source files and openLCA 2.7.0 native modules

claims.text: A second round-trip separates the two by doubling the system target to 0.13 kg while leaving the process quantitative reference at 0.065 kg. The source model now demands twice the activity. Re-importing via JSON-LD restores the 0.13 kg target, whereas this eILCD export path writes no independent system target, causing the importer to fall back to the reference exchange's 0.065 kg. The eILCD-imported model still solves without error, yet its recovered demand is only half of what was originally requested.
claims.scope: Which question a file round-trip preserves; named cases using pinned source files and openLCA 2.7.0 native modules

claims.text: The inventory of the selected CO₂ flow scales directly with the recovered target. Preserving the doubled target in JSON-LD yields approximately 0.673061727 kg, whereas re-importing through eILCD yields approximately 0.336530863 kg. Process coefficients and saved links survived intact; the smaller recovered target reduced the activity level. That ratio documents the behavior of the specific export and import paths tested.
claims.scope: Which question a file round-trip preserves; named cases using pinned source files and openLCA 2.7.0 native modules

claims.text: A separate check distinguishes stored signs from interface display direction. In the background database, the same "municipal waste" flow appears both as a positive input and as a negative output. In this non-regionalized index—which does not split rows by location—both entries collapse into a single row that retains the input flag of whichever exchange is registered first, and the result view uses that input/output flag to flip display signs. Different re-import runs exhibited different summary flags even while inspected process exchange fields, signed coefficients, and inventory quantities remained identical. Because this behavior occurred in both JSON-LD and eILCD and no single root cause was traced here, it cannot be attributed solely to doubling the target or to one file format.
claims.scope: Which question a file round-trip preserves; named cases using pinned source files and openLCA 2.7.0 native modules
caveats: Which exchange was visited first in each run was not traced; source code explains the first-registration rule, but no causal effect of working directory, timestamps, or format on traversal order was measured.

claims.text: Published tool-comparison studies likewise require checking what objects were actually converted. Savioli and colleagues' evaluation of Lavoisier compares EcoSpold 2 and ILCD process data sets while explicitly excluding the eILCD life cycle models examined here. Their study documents provider-field loss and notes that a proper life cycle impact assessment (LCIA) result comparison could not be completed. Such studies show which field changes occur in the tested tools and data sets, whereas verifying activity equivalence in the bottle and injection-molding cases requires inspecting those models and their calculated results directly.
claims.scope: Which question a file round-trip preserves; named cases using pinned source files and openLCA 2.7.0 native modules

claims.text: Having a flow quantity in the inventory does not yet establish how it enters an impact indicator. In openLCA's characterization-factor editor, each record pairs a flow with a factor value, a unit, and a location. All four fields must be verified to know which inventory entry a given number multiplies.
claims.scope: Characterization-factor interface in openLCA 2

claims.text: Calculating an impact category first matches inventory flows to applicable characterization factors and then multiplies them. Even in a non-regionalized setup, matching requires verifying flow identity, unit and property conversions, and geographic applicability—a factor valid only for one location cannot be applied globally by default. The method, version, and category define what is being assessed, while actual factor matching determines which flows enter the sum.
claims.scope: The same numeric zero can arise from different records; named cases using pinned source files and openLCA 2.7.0 native modules

claims.text: When a flow contributes nothing to an impact score, work back from the total to coverage checks. The openLCA manual notes that LCIA Checks list flows not evaluated in a given category, with mapping mismatches being only one possible cause. Once an uncharacterized flow is flagged, one must still determine whether a valid factor exists and applies before explaining why the flow was excluded from the indicator.
claims.scope: Completeness check in the openLCA 2 manual

claims.text: The division of labor between inventory and characterization also explains part of the boundary divergence in agriculture. The English corrigendum republication of European Union (EU) Commission Recommendation (EU) 2021/2279 provides an expert-judgment default split for applied pesticide active ingredients—90% to agricultural soil, 9% to air, and 1% to water—while permitting more specific data when available. The recommendation notes that its USEtox model simulates environmental fate starting from each receiving compartment. By contrast, the ILCD 2010 Handbook generally estimates specific emission pathways leaving managed land. Because one starts by partitioning the applied dose and the other starts from defined field-level emissions, two columns both labeled "kg pesticide" cannot be placed side by side as equivalent.
claims.scope: Comparison of agricultural interfaces in PEF (EU) 2021/2279 R(01) Annex I §4.4.1.4 and ILCD 2010
caveats: Default fractions are not field measurements, do not represent all EF interventions, and do not determine the value of any specific EF 3.1 factor.

claims.text: If an applied active-ingredient dose is q, applying those default fractions with compatible linear characterization factors yields an indicator score of q × (0.90 c(soil) + 0.09 c(air) + 0.01 c(water)), where the three c terms represent factors starting from soil, air, and water respectively. Another model that already estimates compartment-specific emissions must multiply those emissions by factors compatible with its own interface. Interpreting equal scores as model correspondence requires checking emission quantities, starting compartments, and which environmental transport processes are included; a single weighted sum can also coincide accidentally when factors happen to be equal or opposing differences cancel out. Equal applied doses do not establish correspondence, and transport already embedded in a characterization factor cannot be added a second time without verification.
claims.scope: Author's interface derivation from cited PEF pesticide rules and linear characterization
caveats: No real pesticide factors were assigned, no field impacts were estimated, and no product rankings were compared; factors across the two interfaces are not assumed equal.

claims.text: Nor can this division of labor be reduced to "EF always treats applied amounts as emissions". For phosphorus eutrophication, the same recommendation prescribes using water emissions with water-compartment factors when runoff data are available, and allows using applied amounts paired with soil factors that incorporate runoff only when runoff data are lacking. The difference lies in whether transport is estimated in the inventory or absorbed into the characterization factor. Interface choices must therefore be read together with the impact model: defaults cannot be passed off as field measurements, and splitting more processes in the inventory does not by itself guarantee higher accuracy.
claims.scope: Conditional substitution and methodological judgment in PEF (EU) 2021/2279 R(01) Annex I §4.4.1.5
caveats: The conditional substitution for phosphorus does not automatically generalize to all pesticides, nutrients, or environmental pathways.

claims.text: Suppose an inventory contains 3 kg of a given flow. If an applicable characterization factor has been found and confirmed to be zero, the contribution is 3 × 0 = 0. If no applicable factor is known, that flow's contribution remains unknown, and summing the remaining flows produces only a partial total. This arithmetic example clarifies the difference between those two information states; how large the unknown contribution is, or whether it could alter a comparison ranking, requires empirical evidence.
claims.scope: Information states and arithmetic of a hypothetical inventory; not an empirical impact result
caveats: No real environmental impact was calculated; neither the magnitude nor the direction of the unknown term can be inferred from this example.

claims.text: Even locating a factor record with a numeric value of zero does not yet explain what that zero means. ILCD Format 1.1 documentation for the meanValue field recommends that when an elementary flow is known to contribute to an impact topic yet the method provides no factor, the data set should still reference that flow with a value of zero. Such a zero preserves an unresolved missing-factor state. It uses the exact same field and numeral as an evidence-backed zero factor while carrying a completely different meaning.
claims.scope: Zero-placeholder recommendation for the LCIA factor meanValue field in ILCD Format 1.1 (eDoc 3-23-100-263)
caveats: The inspected text is a format recommendation; the presence of a zero row does not prove that any particular real method used it as a placeholder.

claims.text: Real data packages demand one more layer of inspection. In EF 3.1, the inspected freshwater ecotoxicity entry for "aluminium (iii)" to long-term unspecified water carries a zero value, yet its Extensible Markup Language (XML) comment gives no rationale; from that XML alone, one cannot tell whether the zero is a placeholder or reflects an absence of ecological effect. By contrast, the EF 3.1 update report explicitly explains setting certain entries—such as sulfur freshwater ecotoxicity—to zero; that documents the method authors' decision, though it still does not prove zero real-world effect under every conceivable condition. A recorded value, a methodological rationale, and a real-world effect each require their own evidence.
claims.scope: Contrast between selected EF 3.1 zero rows and explicit zero-assignment explanations in JRC130796
caveats: The authors' full rationale and calculation routines for setting zeros were not reproduced; the explanation for sulfur is not attributed to the zero entry for long-term water aluminum.

claims.text: The diagnostic below operates on the system-wide inventory of the air CO₂ flow in the fixed bottle model rather than on the incineration process's emission alone. Its purpose is solely to test whether a factor record is picked up by the solver; pairing that inventory with an artificial coefficient does not create an alternative environmental impact assessment of the bottle.
claims.scope: Input scope and interpretive purpose of the fixed bottle-model diagnostic
caveats: This explains an existing diagnostic quantity and does not execute a new environmental impact method or real product evaluation.

claims.text: The same bottle calculation graph supports a controlled probe of when a factor enters multiplication. Keeping the full inventory intact in openLCA 2.7.0, an artificial single-category diagnostic method with no environmental interpretation is attached to the air CO₂ flow. Setting the author-defined factor to 2 multiplies the approximately 0.336530863 kg inventory to yield 0.673061727 diagnostic units. This positive control confirms that the record is matched and multiplied; the factor 2 itself represents no environmental impact.
claims.scope: The same numeric zero can arise from different records; named cases using pinned source files and openLCA 2.7.0 native modules

claims.text: Having confirmed that a non-zero factor enters the calculation, keep the same category and first change the factor to 0—leaving one zero-valued factor record in the database—and then delete that factor so zero records remain. The inventory is unchanged, yet both native runs produce 0 in the corresponding characterization-matrix cell and 0 for the diagnostic score. At the numeric output layer, the two source states become indistinguishable; telling them apart requires returning to the stored factor records and matching metadata.
claims.scope: The same numeric zero can arise from different records; named cases using pinned source files and openLCA 2.7.0 native modules

claims.text: The archived CML method itself leaves real inventory flows uncharacterized. Freshwater Acenaphthene—the flow used earlier to verify the treatment process's inventory—has no factor record with a matching UUID in that method. Although the inventory records emissions of that substance, the calculation found no matching characterization record for the flow, so its environmental effect cannot be judged to be zero.
claims.scope: The same numeric zero can arise from different records; named cases using pinned source files and openLCA 2.7.0 native modules

claims.text: Reports should allow readers to trace why any flow did not contribute to an indicator. Distinguishing "matched with factor equal to zero", "no applicable factor found", "explicitly not applicable", and "proxy factor applied"—alongside the rationale for each—gives readers the minimum transparency needed. Specific status codes may vary, but readers must be able to separate evaluated flows, unknown flows, and proxy-supported judgments.
claims.scope: Reporting recommendation for characterization-coverage information states; not a verbatim requirement of the cited manual or ISO
caveats: This status classification is a reporting recommendation rather than a verbatim requirement of the cited manual or ISO standards.

claims.text: Whenever an impact contribution reads zero, trace three steps in order: whether the relevant environmental flow is present in the inventory, whether the selected method matched a factor to it, and what value and rationale that matched record carries. A missing record may reflect category inapplicability rather than an important omission, while a zero record requires separating an evidence-backed zero, a documented placeholder, and an unexplained zero. The bottle probe above tested only two author actions—setting a factor to zero and deleting the row—showing that numeric outputs can coincide without explaining why any real method assigns zero. Likewise, the open waste flow and category totals reported in the unlinked-bottle test do not by themselves establish whether that waste flow was characterized; determining that requires the flow's matching record or item-level contribution.
claims.scope: Evidence layering across ILCD Format 1.1, native software controls, and impact-method records
caveats: The reporting statuses are a synthesis recommendation of this monograph and do not claim that all software tools implement these fields.
The characterization status of an open technical flow cannot be inferred from whole-system totals alone; matching or item-level contribution evidence for that row is still required.

claims.text: Alongside category totals, studies should document the method and version, each inventory flow and its location, the matched factor, and the basis for every coverage judgment. Whenever a flow is judged inapplicable or assigned a proxy value, the rationale should be stated explicitly. Neither a similar flow name nor the absence of a region-specific factor is by itself sufficient grounds to substitute another factor. Once software outputs a zero, readers still need these records to interpret what that zero means.
claims.scope: The same numeric zero can arise from different records; named cases using pinned source files and openLCA 2.7.0 native modules

claims.text: In the bottle model, holding reference, links, and allocation constant produced identical activities across two waste encodings. The injection-molding case showed that even when links survive import, calculation can still omit end-of-life treatment. The format round-trips showed that even when all process data remain intact, the recovered system target can shift to a different quantity. Claiming that a model was "preserved" across conversion therefore requires specifying exactly what was verified: flow objects, versions, units, parameters, links, target demand, and characterization mappings.
claims.scope: Reconnecting calculation mechanics to the evaluated service; named cases using pinned source files and openLCA 2.7.0 native modules

claims.text: Once the mechanics of how records enter the solver are clear, the analysis must return to the service being evaluated. Is this material stream actually suitable for that treatment process? Do the manufactured parts and their performance deliver equivalent use? What comparisons can the chosen background data, allocation rules, and impact methods legitimately support? Running a solver reveals what existing records do inside the calculation; determining whether activities are missing or why an inventory flow went uncharacterized requires separate evidence.
claims.scope: Reconnecting calculation mechanics to the evaluated service; named cases using pinned source files and openLCA 2.7.0 native modules

claims.text: Taken together, these checks give "the same model" a concrete operational meaning. Flow objects and environmental interfaces must correspond; the activities actually demanded across process links must correspond; accounting bases and external demands must correspond; and inventory flows must match the starting compartments of characterization factors. When those correspondences hold, changing signs or rescaling accounting bases leaves the inventory invariant; when an interface shifts, a treatment link drops, or a target demand is lost, the model is answering a different question. A coinciding headline score never substitutes for verifying those correspondences—which is also why expanding a process network still requires asking what upstream supplies and downstream disposals remain unlinked, rather than mistaking an algebraically balanced graph for complete coverage.
claims.scope: Synthesis of bounded source comparisons, algebraic conditions, and named native-module observations
caveats: This does not prove universal equivalence across frameworks, universal correctness of any guide, or empirical validity of any real-world model.

claims.text: Even when all modeled exchanges are linked, a process-based life cycle inventory (LCI) can still omit supporting activities. As Suh et al. observe, tracing upstream through selected processes can extend across many tiers while remaining confined to processes already included in the system. If maintenance is never recorded, solving the simultaneous inventory equations reconciles only the inter-process demands already listed and cannot recover the missing maintenance activity. Analysts must first identify which services support the product system and then locate data capable of representing them.
claims.scope: Reprinted text in Suh's 2004 dissertation, Chapter II; page locators follow the dissertation reprint rather than the ACS journal pagination (pp. 657–664).
caveats: Locators follow the fixed dissertation reprint pagination and PDF indexing and must not be conflated with the ACS journal pagination or treated as supplementary material.

claims.text: An input with negligible mass can still carry a substantial environmental burden, and Suh et al. emphasize that many individually small omissions can accumulate to shift overall results. Services such as maintenance are poorly screened by mass entering the product. Whenever cut-off criteria are applied, the study should state which activities were excluded and whether those omissions could alter the comparison at hand.
claims.scope: Argument on cut-off criteria in Section 2 of the Suh (2004) dissertation reprint; not a new universal cut-off threshold.
caveats: This claim draws on the analytical argument in the reprinted text and does not infer current standard requirements from its historical summaries of standards.

claims.text: Consider two distinct data gaps.
